Abstract:
<jats:p>Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) algorithms possess the capability to accelerate the design of novel materials; however, their advancement in materials science is severely hindered by a fundamental deficit of experimental data, commonly referred to as data starvation. Unlike solution-based chemistry, where high-throughput (HT) technologies are a well-established standard, the automated synthesis of solid materials—particularly polymers and multicomponent composites—poses an extreme engineering challenge. Furthermore, the traditional, manual research model is inherently flawed by human bias, notably the systematic non-publication of negative results, which deprives AI models of critical boundary information regarding the design space. This paper is the first in a three-part review series defining the architecture of a fully automated, unbiased “data factory” for closed-loop discovery. This section focuses on the physical foundations of the HT workflow: experimental planning, automated synthesis, and material management. Emphasis is placed on the paradigm shift from classical, discrete Design of Experiments (DoE) to the novel concept of Continuous Gradient DoE. It reviews how robotic platforms utilizing precise gravimetric and volumetric feeders, integrated with extruders and in-line capillary rheology, enable the seamless, high-throughput manufacturing of thermoplastics and composites. Moreover, an innovative approach to sample logistics is presented, redefining classical storage patterns through the implementation of Continuous Material Management. This encompasses direct physical tagging (e.g., inkjet marking on continuous filaments or films), spool-based transport systems, and precise, real-time metadata mapping. As demonstrated, the integration of these systems yields an order-of-magnitude increase in productivity (generating tens of thousands of novel material variants annually), a radical reduction in unit costs, and the production of terabytes of standardized, machine-readable data. Establishing this reliable hardware and analytical infrastructure represents the essential first step toward unlocking the full potential of artificial intelligence in advanced materials engineering.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Additive manufacturing (AM) is revolutionizing the aerospace, transportation, energy, and biomedical fields due to its capacity for rapid production of geometrically complex components. The advancement of alloys for AM is critical to further boost those applications. The first-generation alloys for AM largely rely on conventional commercial alloys that were originally developed under the assumption of near-equilibrium solidification. However, some of these materials are incompatible with the non-equilibrium metallurgical behavior of AM, which may face issues like high crack susceptibility. Thus, the second-generation alloy design for AM builds upon conventional alloy systems by inoculation treatments with alloying elements (e.g., zirconium) or ceramic reinforcements (e.g., titanium carbide) to achieve better material printability and properties. Meanwhile, the limitations of commercial materials underscore the need for developing novel alloys specifically tailored for AM. The third-generation empirical approach for material design adopts a knowledge-driven strategy by leveraging established metallurgical principles and empirical correlations to guide targeted composition optimization. Such trial-and-error strategies for discovering new materials face substantial bottlenecks like long development cycles and high costs. Hence, it has propelled research toward the fourth-generation paradigm—data-driven artificial intelligence (AI) assisted materials design for AM, which is an effective and innovative material solution guided by AM-specific metallurgical features. Advances in AI and robotics will shift the future paradigm of AM-specific alloy design toward an autonomous AI-Lab, which leverages an intelligent AM agent and automated high-throughput AM printing and testing for materials discovery.</jats:p>

Abstract:
The field of materials science stands at a critical inflection point. While laboratory innovations continue to emerge at an unprecedented pace, the traditional timeline from discovery to market in 10–20 years has become an unacceptable bottleneck in addressing urgent technological challenges. We argue that self-driving laboratories (SDLs) represent not merely another step in automation, but a fundamental reimagining of the materials development pipeline. By integrating manufacturing constraints and scalability considerations from the earliest stages of discovery, SDLs can collapse the laboratory-to-factory timeline while improving reproducibility and success rates. This requires abandoning the traditional sequential approach of materials screening, device optimization and manufacturing scale-up; in favor of concurrent cross-scale development. Here, we critically examine current SDL implementations, challenge prevailing assumptions about automation in materials science, and propose a roadmap for truly integrated materials development platforms that could revolutionize how we translate laboratory discoveries into commercial products.

<jats:p>Next-generation autonomous laboratories that combine machine learning, robotic synthesis, and in situ characterization is rapidly emerging as one of the key directions in modern materials science. By integrating active and deep learning algorithms with multi-level datasets ranging from quantum mechanical simulations to high-throughput flow-based experiments, these platforms establish closed-loop frameworks that guide complex nanofabrication processes in real time. Such AI-driven systems lower material and energy consumption, enable the precise design of nanostructures with tailored optical, electronic, and mechanical properties, and create research opportunities that were previously difficult to realize. This review provides a comprehensive overview of self-driving laboratories (SDLs), including their architectures, algorithmic strategies, and practical demonstrations such as the optimization of perovskite nanostructures, the development of nanoparticles for targeted drug delivery, and the synthesis of quantum dots with controlled emission. It also discusses existing methodological limitations, the need for standardized data practices, and challenges related to the integration of in situ techniques, while highlighting the prospects for creating fully digital pipelines for material production, as evidenced by recent autonomous laboratory demonstrations that progressed from initial hypotheses to functional prototypes within remarkably short timeframes.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Metal powders are key to metal additive manufacturing technologies such as powder bed fusion. These powder feedstocks experience a range of forces and physical phenomena both during the powder bed fusion process and additional post-processing stages that can alter their composition and material properties. To evaluate such effects, these powders need to be characterized, tested, and analyzed at critical stages of their lifecycles. This paper provides a review of the current state of the art for powder evaluation methods and their applicability for powder bed fusion production. Methods are categorized by the properties they evaluate, either particulate or bulk properties. Industry standards are identified for each method if applicable and the advantages and disadvantages of each are defined. Effects of these properties on the flowability and spreadability of powders are synthesized and practical management guidelines are defined. This paper aims at providing an overview of powder evaluation for powder bed fusion, practical considerations for the development of powder test and evaluation programs, and provide insights for future research undertakings in the field.

Abstract:
Additive manufacturing and especially the laser-based powder bed fusion (LPBF) with full melting of the powder offers tremendous potential and versatility for manufacturing high quality, complex, precision metal parts. However, for novel powder compositions the LPBF process development is very time consuming and cost intensive due to the layer wise melting and the powder prices. This research work investigates the manufacturing of single and layered multi-material structures in a novel modular lab-scaled LPBF machining system through individual process and material development. In an application example, a multi-material specimen made out of stainless steel 316L and Bronze 90/10 was manufactured in alternating layers. For this approach, a parameter study was performed for each material to investigate the influence of the volumetric energy density (VED) on the specimen density, surface flatness and reduced mixing zone formation. Afterwards, optimized parameters were used to demonstrate the feasibility of the system to produce a multi-material layered 316L-Bronze part.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Metal additive manufacturing (AM) has emerged as a transformative route for producing lightweight, high-precision, and geometrically complex components in aerospace, biomedical, and microelectronic sectors. Among AM technologies, Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) offers exceptional design freedom; however, its widespread adoption particularly for titanium alloys remains constrained by two persistent challenges: shrinkage-induced dimensional deviation and porosity-related performance loss. In LPBF-processed Ti-6Al-4V, residual linear deviation typically falls within 0.1–0.8% when geometric compensation, preheating, and support strategies are implemented, while raw, uncompensated shrinkage is more commonly reported in the range of 1.2–2.0%, especially for thin-wall or thermally constrained geometries. Volumetric contraction (approximately 2–6%) may remain significant depending on part architecture and localized thermal accumulation. Concurrently, gas-induced and lack-of-fusion pores continue to undermine fatigue resistance and dimensional reliability. Research into process optimization, thermal management, and post-processing such as Hot Isostatic Pressing (HIP), vacuum sintering, and stress-relief annealing has improved density and mechanical integrity, while recent developments in AI-assisted monitoring, physics-informed models, and digital-twin frameworks are redefining defect prediction and control. Drawing on more than 100 peer-reviewed studies, this review synthesizes mechanism-driven insights and outlines a forward-looking roadmap, demonstrating how hybrid processing, real-time sensing, and data-centric control collectively advance the pathway toward defect-minimized, industrial-scale manufacturing of titanium components.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>Metal additive manufacturing (AM) enables components with high geometric complexity and functional integration; however, these advantages are realized only when topology optimization (TO) aligns with AM-specific constraints. This review examines TO strategies for metal AM, with emphasis on laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) as the most established industrial route. It categorizes and assesses density-based methods, level-set approaches, and lattice or architected-material optimization, focusing on how each captures manufacturability (overhang limits, minimum feature size, surface roughness), physics (residual stress, thermal distortion), and AM-induced anisotropy. It further distinguishes algorithms that embed constraints directly into the TO loop from workflows that rely on post-optimization repair. It discusses implications for robustness and transferability across machines and alloys. Experimental and numerical evidence for titanium alloys, aluminum alloys, nickel-based superalloys, and stainless steels is synthesized to relate design decisions and processing conditions to reported gains in stiffness-to-weight ratio, strength, fatigue performance, and buy-to-fly efficiency. Persistent gaps include validation under realistic load spectra, uncertainty quantification, standardized benchmarks, microstructure-informed objectives, and sustainability metrics. Beyond synthesizing existing TO formulations and constraints, this review contributes a criteria-based decision structure linking TO method selection, constraint strategy, and process-physics coupling and identifies four inherent paradoxes defining the field’s open challenges.</jats:p>

Jochen Schanz, Nabirul Islam, David Kolb, David K. Harrison, Anjali K. M. De Silva, Dagmar Goll, Gerhard Schneider, and Harald Riegel. Individual process development of single and multi-material laser melting in novel modular laser powder bed fusion system. Progress in Additive Manufacturing, 7:481-493, Apr 2022. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s40964-022-00276-9, doi:10.1007/s40964-022-00276-9. This article has 17 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt describes research-oriented LPBF powder delivery approaches, but it does not provide a complete comparison of hoppers, cartridges, dose-on-demand feeders, metering rollers, vibratory feeders, screw feeders, or slot feeders, nor does it state a numerical powder quantity required per layer. It contrasts industrial machines, which generally use a single powder reservoir and relatively large build chambers, with more flexible research systems designed for novel materials and multi-material processing. Reported research concepts include several powder dispenser systems for autonomous material selection, ultrasonic dispenser nozzles for local powder deposition, and an integrated powder mixer. For multi-material fabrication, another cited concept uses a recoating roller or blade together with a building-platform cleaning system intended to separate different powders for reuse. A vacuum chamber has also been developed to deposit two materials independently for micro-scale multi-material parts. The featured modular lab-scale system supports different laser sources, optical arrangements, sensors, and actuators, as well as individual mixed powder compositions and layered multi-material parts, while requiring only a minimum amount of powder. The demonstrated example alternated 316L stainless steel and Bronze 90/10 layers. Layer evenness is emphasized because it helps maintain consistent powder-layer thickness and reduce mixing zones.

## pqac-00000027

From text 'revanur2024novelscanstrategies pages 18-22'.

Ramkumar Revanur. Novel scan strategies for selective laser melting. Text, Jan 2024. URL: https://doi.org/10.17638/03176890, doi:10.17638/03176890. This article has 2 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt identifies two powder supply approaches used in LPBF machines: gas-recirculating powder delivery systems and gravity-fed systems. The excerpt indicates that preheating and thermal management can improve tungsten LPBF, but their benefits are strongly limited by oxidation. Laser pre-scanning combined with plate insulation increased the mean fusion-zone penetration depth to 88 µm, compared with approximately 72 µm for the control after anomalous defect-related measurements were excluded. It also significantly improved interface density and reduced cracking and large defect bands. A heated-bed module operated successfully at a 600 °C target, maintaining temperature within 5 °C; the study also examined 400 °C and 600 °C plates, alongside room-temperature processing. At 600 °C, however, oxidation became severe: a blue oxide layer, identified as typical of WO3, formed rapidly and re-formed after laser ablation. Oxide increased weld-pool surface tension, causing balling, poor wetting, substantial track undulations, and high measurement variability. Oxide vaporization and redeposition were also possible. Thus, higher plate temperatures may enlarge melt pools and reduce thermal gradients, but they require improved atmosphere control and insulation because residual oxygen and oxidation can degrade powder-bed and melt-track quality.

Article
Effects of Platform Pre-Heating and
Thermal-Treatment Strategies on Properties of
AlSi10Mg Alloy Processed by Selective Laser Melting

Riccardo Casati 1    , Milad Hamidi Nasab 1    , Mauro Coduri 2    , Valeria Tirelli 3
and Maurizio Vedani 1,*

  1  Department of Mechanical Engineering, Politecnico di Milano, 20156 Milan, Italy;
      riccardo.casati@polimi.it (R.C.); milad.hamidi@polimi.it (M.H.N.)
  2   ESRF, European Syncrotron Radiation Facility, 38043 Grenoble, France; mauro.coduri@esrf.fr
  3   Aidro S.r.l, 21020 Taino, Italy; valeria.tirelli@aidro.it
 *   Correspondence: maurizio.vedani@polimi.it; Tel.: +39-02-2399-8230

 Received: 12 October 2018; Accepted: 13 November 2018; Published: 15 November 2018


 Abstract: The AlSi10Mg alloy was processed by selective laser melting using both hot- and
 cold-build platforms. The investigation was aimed at deﬁning suitable platform pre-heating and
 post-process thermal treatment strategies, taking into consideration the peculiar microstructures
 generated. Microstructural analyses, differential scanning calorimetry, and high-resolution diffraction
 from synchrotron radiation, showed that in the cold platform as-built condition, the amount of
 supersaturated Si was higher than in hot platform samples. The best hardness and tensile performance
 were achieved upon direct aging from cold platform-printed alloys. The hot platform strategy led
 to a loss in the aging response, since the long processing times spent at high temperature induced
 a substantial overaging effect, already in the as-built samples.  Finally, the standard T6 temper
 consisting of post-process solution annealing followed by artiﬁcial aging, resulted in higher ductility
 but lower mechanical strength.


 Keywords: selective laser melting; AlSi10Mg alloy; processing temperature; aging treatment




1. Introduction

   Due to large freedom in shaping and high material usage efﬁciency, selective laser melting
(SLM) is attracting a great interest for a large number of industrial applications requiring near-net
shape manufacturing of light components. SLM allows generating parts by selectively scanning
powdered metals with a laser beam, so as to produce layer by layer solid volumes after melting
and solidiﬁcation [1,2]. AlSi10Mg and AlSi7Mg alloys are amongst the most popular materials for
light structures built by SLM. They are selected among the traditional foundry alloys featuring good
castability and well-known solidiﬁcation behavior [3–5].
    The trend toward increased lightness and higher load-bearing capacity is now pushing for higher
material strength, which can be achieved either by alternative Al alloy formulations or by optimized
thermal treatments of current materials. High-strength precipitation hardenable Al-Zn-Mg-Cu and
Al-Cu-Mg-Si alloys offer large opportunities to achieve high mechanical performances, but their
processability is often limited due to hot-cracking phenomena occurring during the last stages of the
rapid solidiﬁcation induced by SLM [6,7]. An alternative approach, aimed at raising the strength of the
above easily processable Al-Si-Mg alloys, is to optimize their post-process thermal treatments, trying
to exploit, as much as possible, the supersaturation of the solid solution and the ﬁne cellular structure
brought about by the rapid solidiﬁcation and cooling induced by SLM.



Metals 2018, 8, 954; doi:10.3390/met8110954                                         www.mdpi.com/journal/metalsMetals 2018, 8, 954                                                                                         2 of 12



    From the recent literature, there is evidence that several kinds of post-process heat treatments can
be considered. Stress relieving is often carried out on as-built AlSi10Mg parts at temperatures of 300 ◦C
for 2 h [8–11], but investigations showing the effectiveness of annealing treatments at temperatures as
low as 200 ◦C are also available [10,12]. Such treatments lead to a substantial increase in alloy ductility
and a concurrent drop in strength.
     Solution-annealing treatments and solution annealing followed by aging (T6-like thermal
treatments) have been also investigated on AlSi10Mg and AlSi7Mg alloys processed by SLM, in order to
modify the properties of the as-built materials [3,5,9,11,13–19]. It was shown that the standard solution
annealing, followed by water quenching and artiﬁcial aging, replaces the ﬁne α-Al cells, and the Si
network segregated at their boundaries into coarser grains and globular Si particles. Evidence of laser
tracks, and of the related heat-affected zones, also disappeared during solution annealing [3,9,13,15,19].
Also, in this case, fracture elongation signiﬁcantly improves, but hardness, yield strength, and ultimate
tensile strength drop down to values lower than those of the as-built material.
   An interesting database about the mechanical properties available in literature for the AlSi10Mg
alloy, processed by SLM, was given in a recent paper by Tang and Pistorious [20], who showed a large
variability of the achieved performance depending on sample orientation, processing parameters,
and heat treatment condition. Maamoun and co-workers [21] published a research study on thermal
post-processing of AlSi10Mg alloy after SLM, and supplied conclusive suggestions in the form of a
microstructure/microhardness map on possible options for post-processing treatments. However,
it must be considered that the adoption of the aging treatment was evaluated only after the standard
solution-annealing treatment, according to conventional T6-like treatment used in cast and wrought
Al alloys.
    The aging response of an A357 (AlSi7Mg) alloy produced by SLM was specifically investigated
in [18]. Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) and microhardness analyses showed that SLM-processed
samples feature the same precipitation sequence of the corresponding cast alloy, by the sequential
formation of Mg-Mg, Si-Si, and Mg-Si co-clusters, β”, β’, and β (Mg2Si) phases, along with the
precipitation of Si [22–24]. Moreover, it was demonstrated that the as-built and the solution-annealed
and quenched samples experienced, substantially, the same precipitation sequence when subjected
to direct aging. The as-built condition can, therefore, be considered as fully appropriate for an
effective dispersion strengthening process by direct artiﬁcial aging, without the need of any post-SLM
solution-annealing treatment.
     Further information on aging behavior of supersaturated alloys generated by rapid solidiﬁcation
can be obtained from a recent work published by Marola and co-authors [25]. Their comparative
study on an AlSi10Mg alloy, processed by SLM, copper mold casting, and melt spinning, showed
that extensive Si supersaturation takes place in rapidly solidiﬁed alloys. At the early stages of aging,
the supersaturated Si was able to precipitate, leading to broad DSC signals that overlap to those
originally assigned to β” formation. These results are consistent with XRD data supplied by Li and
co-workers in their study on effects of heat treatments of AlSi10Mg alloy produced by SLM [13].
    The above observations suggest that the peculiar microstructure of Al alloys after the rapid
solidiﬁcation and cooling conditions inherited by SLM could be considered as a proﬁtable starting
point for the design of optimized aging treatments in additively manufactured Al alloys. The present
paper is, therefore, aimed at evaluating the beneﬁts of different possible heat treatment strategies on
an AlSi10Mg alloy. Opportunities offered by SLM processing on room-temperature building platforms,
rather than on hot building platforms, are also investigated. In the ﬁrst scenario, the supersaturated
solid solution of as-built material is exploited as the starting condition for subsequent aging whereas,
in the latter, the strengthening action of a possible in situ aging treatment is investigated.

2. Materials and Methods

   An EOS M290 SLM system was adopted to process gas-atomized AlSi10Mg powders according
to the parameters supplied in Table 1. The table also shows that a set of samples, labeled as HP,Metals 2018, 8, 954                                                                                         3 of 12


was produced by depositing powder layers on a preheated build platform at 160 ◦C, whereas a second
set, labeled as CP, was printed without any preheating. The speciﬁc temperature level of 160 ◦C,
for the hot platform, was selected in order to reproduce the usual aging temperature adopted for
cast AlSi10Mg alloys. It should be considered that information about the build platform temperature
are not always supplied in the experimental descriptions of published investigations. Examples of
35 ◦C [8,10,26–28], 100 ◦C [13], and 200 ◦C [21] platform processing are available in literature.

messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-00)

| Alloy system | Preheat temperature range (°C) | Key effects on cracking | Key effects on residual stress | Key effects on microstructure/properties | Source |
|---|---:|---|---|---|---|
| AlSi10Mg | 35; 150; 160; 170; 200 | Generally not crack-limited; preheating lowers thermal gradients, but its principal consequence in this range is thermal ageing rather than crack suppression. | Expected reduction in thermal gradients and stress; quantitative reduction not established in the cited experiments. | At 150 °C, Si and strengthening β″ precipitates form in situ; subsequent T5 response becomes marginal. At 160–170 °C, long exposure causes height-dependent ageing and over-ageing near the plate; at 170 °C, peak hardness occurred about 40 mm above the plate after approximately 10 h equivalent exposure. Hot-platform material retains less supersaturated Si and has reduced subsequent ageing response. At 200 °C, Si precipitates within Al cells and yield strength may decline. Literature also reports processing at 35 °C. | (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000007, pqac-00000046) |
| EN AW 6182 / AlSi1MgZr (6xxx) | 400–500 | Hot-crack density falls strongly with increasing temperature; columnar-to-equiaxed transition begins near 400 °C. At 500 °C, optimized parameters produced crack-free specimens with density greater than 99%. | Reduced gradients and associated thermal stresses are the proposed mechanism; no direct residual-stress value was reported. | Fully equiaxed grain structure at 500 °C; preheat temperature had a stronger effect on cracking than hatch distance or focus position. | (pqac-00000006) |
| AA7075 / EN AW 7075 (7xxx) | 25, 100, 200, 400 | Cracks persisted throughout. Preheating at 100–200 °C did not significantly reduce crack density; at 400 °C, cracking changed to columnar networks and was not eliminated. Separate work reported 99.8% density at 200 °C without crack suppression. | Little change at 100–200 °C; 400 °C promoted thermal relaxation and lower local strain/dislocation density, although cracking itself can release stored strain energy. | Hardness peaked at 100 °C and declined at 200–400 °C; the 400 °C condition altered grain orientation and promoted segregation-sensitive crack paths. Reported processing loss was approximately 1 wt.% Zn and 0.3 wt.% Mg, largely independent of preheat temperature. | (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000003, pqac-00000004) |

{"artifact_type": "table", "description": "Create a table of heater technologies for LPBF build plate preheating. Columns: Technology, Maximum Temperature Achieved (°C), System Description, Advantages, Limitations, Source. Include:
- Resistive cartridge heaters: typical ≤200°C on commercial machines, up to 700°C custom (Field 2020, 6×100W 24V cartridge heaters, 60×45×50mm build volume, W plate, K-type thermocouples, ±5°C control, 30min dwell)
- Ceramic (AlN) heater: 3kW, reached 395°C heater / 374°C plate, insulation 44% efficient, redesign predicted 650°C (Ramulifho 2022)
- Induction helical coil: >800°C sustained 450min ±10°C, max >840°C (Caprio, Project Grisù), pancake coil up to 1000°C (Hagedorn)
- Laser diode: 4×1.25kW diodes at 625°C (Ramulifho citation)
- CO2/Nd:YAG laser: 1500-2500°C for ceramics only
- EOS M290 HT system: 900°C base plate + 1200°C surface heating, IR camera, O2 < 200 ppm (Wartbichler 2022)"}

### Artifact (ID artifact-01)

| Technology | Maximum temperature achieved (°C) | System description | Advantages | Limitations | Source |
|---|---:|---|---|---|---|
| Resistive cartridge heaters | Typically ≤200 commercial; 700 custom | Six 100 W, 24 V cartridges heated a 5 mm tungsten plate over a 60 × 45 × 50 mm build volume. Two central K-type thermocouples provided ±5 °C switching control; a 30 min dwell promoted uniformity. A ceramic insert reduced downward heat loss. | Simple, compact, inexpensive and readily controlled; well suited to a swappable Ø25–50 mm aluminium-alloy plate module. | Conductive losses into the piston and frame can dominate; adjacent components require independent thermocouples and safety cut-offs. Uniformity depends on heater layout and soak time. | (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000018) |
| AlN resistive ceramic heater | 395 heater; 374 plate; 548.8 insulated test; redesigned system predicted ≈650 | A 3 kW, 290 × 290 × 23 mm aluminium-nitride heater was evaluated beneath a metal substrate. Tested insulation was only 44% efficient; redesign reduced metallic heat bridges without increasing heater power. | Flat heater provides high areal power density and potentially better plate uniformity than discrete cartridges. | Brittle and thermally stressed; poor insulation and contacting metal structures produced a 21 °C heater-to-plate drop and prevented the original system reaching its 600 °C target. | (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000014) |
| Induction, helical coil (“Project Grisù”) | >840; 800 sustained for 450 min at approximately ±10 | A roughly 100 kHz helical copper coil surrounded the descending substrate assembly. A 48 V, 20 A zero-voltage-switching supply heated an embedded steel susceptor or conductive substrate; water-cooled exchangers protected the piston and drive. | Fast response; reaches temperatures impractical for ordinary resistive systems; coil geometry maintains heating with build height. At 800 °C, TiAl cracking was suppressed and apparent density exceeded 99%. | Requires conductive substrate or susceptor, electromagnetic compatibility engineering and water cooling. ON/OFF control was less stable below 500 °C; direct induction effects on loose metallic powder were not fully resolved. | (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000019, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021) |
| Induction, pancake coil | Up to ≈1000 | Planar induction coil beneath or around the build substrate, reported as an earlier high-temperature LPBF approach. | Very high achievable plate temperature and rapid, contactless energy delivery. | Heating effectiveness falls with build height unless the coil follows or surrounds the build; nonuniform coupling, shielding and cooling complicate implementation. | (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000022) |
| High-power diode-laser preheating | 625 | Four 1.25 kW diode lasers supplied auxiliary surface heating during LPBF. | Non-contact, dynamically addressable heating; reported to reduce residual stress substantially in 316L bridge specimens. | Adds optical complexity and another high-power beam path; absorption and uniformity depend on powder condition and surface geometry, with possible interference from plume and condensate. | (pqac-00000009) |
| CO₂ or Nd:YAG laser preheating of ceramics | ≥1600 CO₂; approximately 1500–2500 Nd:YAG | A separate laser pre-scans or continuously heats the powder surface immediately before melting; cited demonstrations concern ceramic SLM rather than conventional metallic build plates. | Delivers extreme local temperatures without heating the piston and seals; can reduce ceramic thermal shock and cracking. | Not a demonstrated general-purpose metal build-plate heater. Large gradients, optical-access demands, powder disturbance and high energy use make it unsuitable as the primary 200–500 °C aluminium-platform solution. | (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000015) |
| EOS M 290 HT combined plate and surface/chamber heating | 900 base plate; 1200 upper powder-bed layer | High-temperature M 290 modification combining base heating with heating of the uppermost bed layer. It incorporated IR-camera monitoring, chamber cooling, data logging and inert-gas purification maintaining O₂ below 200 ppm. | Maintains thermal control at greater build heights, where base heating alone becomes ineffective; enabled dense, crack-free TiAl processing and in-situ microstructure control. | High capital and systems complexity; severe thermal loads on optics, seals, gas hardware and sensors; far beyond what is required for routine aluminium screening. | (pqac-00000023) |

function.arguments:
{"artifact_type": "table", "description": "Create a ranked list of concrete design choices for a desktop alloy-screening LPBF machine. Rank by priority/impact. Include columns: Rank, Design Choice, Quantitative Target/Specification, Rationale (with key literature evidence), and Implementation Notes. Cover approximately 15-20 items:

1. Heated build plate with resistive cartridge heaters, target 500°C for 6xxx crack-free processing
2. Interchangeable build plate sizes Ø25mm and Ø50mm with zero-point kinematic coupling
3. Thermal isolation of heater from piston (ceramic insert, water cooling, components <100°C)
4. Quick-swap hopper cartridges in 3 sizes (~25, 50, 100 cm³)
5. Servo ball-screw recoater with adjustable gap
6. Vacuum-purgeable argon chamber <200 ppm O2
7. Temperature measurement: K-type thermocouples beneath plate ±5°C, IR camera optional
8. Plate registration via precision pin + screw (Zanini approach) or zero-point clamping
9. Powder containment walls matching plate diameter
10. Argon stabilization ≥4h before high-temp heating
11. Replaceable laser window cover slide
12. Automated plate removal interface (magnetic or kinematic, robot-compatible)
13. Closed powder recovery with sieving
14. Chamber cleaning access (condensate removal)
15. Multi-material hopper option
16. Data logging and API for autonomous lab integration
17. Build plate material: Al alloy for Al builds, Ti-6Al-4V for high-temp
18. Piston seals rated to max plate temp (silicone <200°C, PTFE <250°C, graphite >500°C)
19. Temperature uniformity: ±5°C across Ø50mm plate after 30min soak
20. Minimum powder per layer: ~1 cm³ for Ø50mm plate at 50µm layer"}

messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-02)

| Rank | Design choice | Quantitative target/specification | Rationale with key evidence | Implementation notes |
|---:|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Modular heated build-plate cassette | Routine module: ambient–200 °C; high-temperature module: ambient–500 °C plate, with heater capability ≥550 °C | AlSi10Mg undergoes useful in-situ ageing around 150–170 °C but can over-age during long exposure; crack-free, fully equiaxed EN AW-6182 was demonstrated at 500 °C and >99% density. AA7075 was not made crack-free even at 400 °C, so 500 °C capability is valuable but not universally sufficient. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000003, pqac-00000006, pqac-00000007) | Use replaceable heater cassettes rather than forcing one assembly to span every regime. A 3–6-cartridge symmetric pattern is appropriate for Ø50 mm; derate heater watt density in vacuum and provide independent over-temperature protection. |
| 2 | Interchangeable Ø25 and Ø50 mm build modules | Ø25 mm screening insert and Ø50 mm validation insert; common Z datum and coupling; recommended remount repeatability ≤10 µm in Z and ≤25 µm in X–Y; plate flatness ≤20 µm | A published modular research system used a Ø40 mm substrate and very small powder quantities. A MySINT100 plate used twelve Ø12 mm removable inserts with precision registration, showing that small, replaceable build interfaces are practical. (pqac-00000045, pqac-00000050) | Swap the complete plate, containment sleeve and upper piston seal together. Treat the dimensional tolerances as design targets requiring gauge-R&R validation, not as values directly established by the cited literature. |
| 3 | Thermally isolate heater from Z piston and guides | Ceramic break beneath heater; cooled radiation shield; keep ball screw, encoder, guide bearings and ordinary seals <70–100 °C at a 500 °C plate | A custom cartridge-heated module used a ceramic insert. The high-temperature induction system used three water-cooled exchangers and targeted vulnerable components below 100 °C; motor and transmission limits were about 70 °C. Poor insulation prevented a 3 kW ceramic-heater system from reaching its 600 °C target. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000019, pqac-00000020) | Minimize metallic cross-section between hot cassette and piston, use reflective shields and water-cooled intercepts, and monitor both sides of the thermal break. Interlock Z motion and heating on coolant flow and return temperature. |
| 4 | Reproducible plate registration and clamping | Three-point kinematic or zero-point coupling; one axial clamp; no overconstraint; target ≤10 µm Z repeatability and ≤0.02° tilt | Zero-point systems provide rapid, reproducible fixation. The MySINT100 research plate used cylindrical pockets, precision pins and reverse-side screws to align removable inserts. (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000045) | Use three hardened contacts or a cone–groove–flat arrangement outside the hottest zone. Avoid relying on magnets alone above about 200 °C; provide a positive mechanical lock and presence/lock sensors. |
| 5 | Closed Ø25/Ø50 powder-containment sleeves | Sleeve ID matched to plate with radial running clearance approximately 0.05–0.15 mm at room temperature; leakage gap after thermal expansion ≤0.10–0.20 mm | Circular platforms limit powder dispersion and simplify contained handling. Small modular systems obtain their powder savings by restricting the entire filled cross-section, not merely by placing a small plate in a large bed. (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000050) | Make sleeve, plate and seal a removable build module. Calculate hot clearance using the actual sleeve and plate coefficients of expansion; add an annular overflow collection groove outside the seal. |
| 6 | Dual-zone temperature measurement and control | At least two embedded K- or N-type thermocouples under the Ø50 mm plate plus one cold-side safety sensor; control stability ±5 °C; independent hard trip | A cartridge-heated tungsten module controlled temperature within ±5 °C using two central K-type thermocouples. Inductive TiAl heating sustained 800 °C for 450 min with approximately ±10 °C oscillation. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000016) | Calibrate sensors in the assembled cassette. Place control sensors at center and near the edge; use a separate thermocouple and safety relay for over-temperature shutdown. An IR camera is useful for validation but requires emissivity correction. |
| 7 | Verify plate-temperature uniformity before every alloy campaign | Target center-to-edge variation ≤±5 °C over Ø50 mm after a ≥30 min soak; map at ambient, 170, 300 and 500 °C | A 30 min dwell was used to improve consistency in a custom heated bed, and ±5 °C was its switching criterion. High-temperature systems use IR-camera monitoring because a single underside thermocouple does not prove surface uniformity. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000023) | Validate with a temporary multi-thermocouple calibration plate or calibrated IR camera. Store the uniformity map and thermal-expansion correction with each cassette’s machine-readable ID. |
| 8 | Vacuum-purgeable, low-oxygen argon chamber | Demonstration minimum: O₂ <200 ppm; preferred aluminium screening target before exposure: <100 ppm and stable; trend dew point or moisture independently | The EOS high-temperature TiAl system maintained oxygen below 200 ppm with gas purification. Tungsten work showed that residual oxygen at 600 °C rapidly formed blue WO₃, causing poor wetting and balling. (pqac-00000023, pqac-00000039, pqac-00000040) | Position the O₂ sensor in a cooled bypass rather than above the hot plate. Interlock laser and heater against oxygen, flow and chamber-pressure limits; log peak O₂ during recoating and heating. |
| 9 | Quick-swap sealed hopper cartridges | Nominal useful capacities about 25, 50 and 100 cm³; residual powder after removal <1% of cartridge capacity; keyed identity and sealed valves | Research systems use accessible rotating reservoirs and can operate with as many as four powders; rapid reservoir replacement reduces contamination and material demand. Industrial powder changes can otherwise require up to two days. (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000050) | Use identical docking geometry with interchangeable cartridge bodies. Include RFID or barcode identification, tare mass, lot number, alloy lockout and a normally closed bottom slot or metering valve. Validate repeatability gravimetrically for each powder. |
| 10 | Servo ball-screw recoater with programmable dosing gap | Layer settings 20–100 µm; Z/recoater positioning resolution ≤2–5 µm; gap repeatability ≤5 µm; programmable speed and torque/force trip | Powder delivery is volumetric and layer consistency depends strongly on the wiper-to-bed datum. A modular system deposited 50 µm layers and recoated in about 5 s. (pqac-00000027, pqac-00000050) | Provide interchangeable soft polymer, ceramic and hardened-metal blades. Record motor current or force to detect caking, protrusions and collisions, and use a bed image before and after every pass. |
| 11 | Right-size the dose per layer rather than dumping a fixed 1 cm³ | Ø50 mm × 50 µm geometric layer volume = 0.098 cm³; initial commanded dose approximately 0.2–0.4 cm³ including packing and overflow; 1 cm³ should be an upper calibration range, not the normal minimum | A Ø40 mm system required about 628 mm³ to fill a 0.5 mm-high bed, consistent with simple area × height geometry, and approximately 791 mm³ after accounting for consolidation into parts. (pqac-00000050) | Calibrate delivered mass versus actuator motion for every powder. Dose only the quantity needed to fill the layer plus a measured safety factor; collect and weigh overflow to close the powder mass balance. |
| 12 | Temperature-compatible piston sealing | Keep elastomeric dynamic seals on the cold side <100–150 °C; use PTFE-based seals only in cooled regions; use graphite, metal labyrinth or replaceable clearance seals adjacent to a 500 °C sleeve | High-temperature LPBF prototypes protect ordinary mechanics by cooling them below 100 °C rather than exposing polymer seals to the bed temperature. (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000020) | Do not interpret generic silicone or PTFE material limits as acceptable dynamic-seal temperatures in oxygen-sensitive powder service. Prefer a hot-side labyrinth/graphite wiper backed by a cooled, conventional vacuum seal. |
| 13 | Plate material matched to experiment | Aluminium-alloy plate for routine Al builds; plate thickness about 8–15 mm for Ø50 mm; optional Ti-6Al-4V or steel/susceptor cassette for >500 °C induction work | Using compatible Al substrates improves thermal and metallurgical similarity for Al screening. The induction prototype selected Ti-6Al-4V because its electrical and thermal behavior allowed effective high-temperature coupling; custom tungsten work used a 5 mm W plate. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000019) | Maintain separate, serialized plate families to prevent cross-contamination. Verify that the plate alloy does not bias grain-refiner chemistry or dilute first-layer composition. |
| 14 | Robot-compatible plate/build-module removal | Repeatable external grasp features; positive lock state; plate/module mass preferably <5 kg; presence confirmation by two independent sensors | Airlocks and rapid-transfer ports shorten plate exchange, while zero-point clamping and common robotic interfaces support automated LPBF-to-post-processing transfer. (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000048) | Prefer a mechanically latched kinematic coupling over magnetic retention alone. Add fiducials, a temperature-permissive signal, load-cell confirmation of pickup and a sealed transport canister for reactive powder. |
| 15 | Closed powder recovery and sieving | Sealed recovery bottle; inert or enclosed sieve matched to feedstock, commonly 63 µm for nominal 15–45 µm powder; recovered, overflow and waste masses logged separately | Automated sieving and recirculation reduce operator exposure and handling time. Multi-material recovery may require separation by size, density or magnetic response and is not automatically contamination-free. (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000025, pqac-00000050) | For novel alloys, default to quarantine rather than immediate reuse. Sample recovered powder for O, H, particle-size distribution and chemistry; never combine different experiments without analytical release. |
| 16 | Removable condensate liners and exchangeable window cover | Tool-less chamber liners; sacrificial optical cover slide or carousel with at least 3–10 indexed positions; transmission check before each build | High-temperature and laser processes create spatter, nanoparticles and volatile condensate; optical contamination threatens fixed-scanner repeatability, while fast-change interfaces reduce downtime. (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000025) | Use an angled, cooled cover slide and monitor laser transmission with a reference photodiode. Treat Al/Mg-rich condensate as reactive combustible waste; remove it using grounded tools or closed HEPA extraction, never dry compressed air. |
| 17 | Chamber geometry designed for automated cleaning | Full line-of-sight access to bed, overflow, gas ducts and window shield; removable smooth liners; internal corner radius ≥5 mm; no blind powder traps | Powder replacement can dominate changeover time, and automatic handling is valuable only if residual powder and soot can be verified absent. Automated powder systems and rapid-transfer concepts specifically target this downtime. (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000025) | Provide grounded vacuum ports, wipeable surfaces and replaceable gas-flow straighteners. Use cameras, differential pressure, gravimetry and particle-count or swab verification before releasing a different alloy. |
| 18 | Optional multi-material feeder module | Two to four independently removable reservoirs; composition changes by discrete layers initially; changeover target ≤3 min after validation | A modular system handled up to four powder types, changed accessible reservoirs in under 3 min and demonstrated alternating 316L/bronze layers. Double-hopper/mixing and ultrasonic local-deposition concepts also exist. (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000050) | Keep multi-material hardware optional because it greatly increases cross-contamination risk. Begin with whole-layer changes; add local deposition only after proving cleaning, dosing and composition uniformity. |
| 19 | Machine API, provenance and autonomous-lab interface | Timestamped API for plate ID, hopper ID, O₂, pressure, flow, temperatures, recoater current, layer images, laser job and interlocks; command acknowledgement and state confirmation for every step | Proposed autonomous AM laboratories combine multi-hopper printing, robotic transfer, heat treatment and automated characterization using equipment APIs, safety interlocks and supervisory agents. (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000030, pqac-00000031) | Use a deterministic state machine beneath any AI scheduler. Expose read-only telemetry broadly but restrict hazardous commands; require physical interlocks, signed recipes, audit trails and human-defined stopping conditions. |
| 20 | Require production-machine correlation builds | At least three matched coupons per alloy on Ø25/50 mm and production-scale plates; match layer time, scan strategy, gas-flow direction and thermal history; predefined equivalence limits for density, crack density, grain size and hardness | Small beds change plate thermal mass, lateral heat loss, inter-layer time and part spacing. AlSi10Mg preheating creates build-height/time-dependent ageing, and changing local thermal history alters microstructure; therefore small-plate results are screening evidence, not automatic production qualification. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000003, pqac-00000032) | Include thermal witness coupons and vary specimen spacing deliberately. Transfer promising parameters using melt-pool dimensions and measured thermal history, then re-optimize on the production machine rather than relying only on nominal volumetric energy density. |

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name
        - OverallStatus: Trial status

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):
        - InterventionOtherName (0.75): Alternative intervention names
        - Phase (0.65): Trial phase
        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1
        - PHASE1: Phase 1
        - PHASE2: Phase 2
        - PHASE3: Phase 3
        - PHASE4: Phase 4
        - NA: Not Applicable

    StandardAge:
        - CHILD: Child
        - ADULT: Adult
        - OLDER_ADULT: Older Adult

    Status:
        - RECRUITING: Currently recruiting participants
        - ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING: Active but not recruiting
        - COMPLETED: Study completed
        - ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION: Enrolling by invitation only
        - NOT_YET_RECRUITING: Not yet recruiting
        - SUSPENDED: Study suspended
        - TERMINATED: Study terminated
        - WITHDRAWN: Study withdrawn
        - AVAILABLE: Available
        - NO_LONGER_AVAILABLE: No longer available
        - TEMPORARILY_NOT_AVAILABLE: Temporarily not available
        - APPROVED_FOR_MARKETING: Approved for marketing
        - WITHHELD: Withheld
        - UNKNOWN: Unknown status

    StudyType:
        - INTERVENTIONAL: Interventional studies
        - OBSERVATIONAL: Observational studies
        - EXPANDED_ACCESS: Expanded access studies

    PrimaryPurpose:
        - TREATMENT: Treatment
        - PREVENTION: Prevention
        - DIAGNOSTIC: Diagnostic
        - ECT: Educational/Counseling/Training
        - SUPPORTIVE_CARE: Supportive Care
        - SCREENING: Screening
        - HEALTH_SERVICES_RESEARCH: Health Services Research
        - BASIC_SCIENCE: Basic Science
        - DEVICE_FEASIBILITY: Device Feasibility

    InterventionType:
        - BEHAVIORAL: Behavioral interventions
        - BIOLOGICAL: Biological interventions

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string encoding an object with an "objectives" list;
never pass objectives separately.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'
or 'filing'. Only necessary to set if after and/or before are set.

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.description:
Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.
This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,
but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

text_name_list.description:
A list of up to 10 text names to read.
These text names can be any valid text names retrieved by other tools.
text_name_list.title: Text Name List

info.name: update_plan

Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

plan_objective_id.description: The id of the objective to update.
plan_objective_id.title: Plan Objective Id

A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.

info.name: collect_cited_papers_in_evidence
info.description:
Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?

Use the tools to answer the question: We are designing a small, research-grade (desktop) laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) machine for screening new aluminium alloys from small powder batches: AlSi10Mg-type alloys, Al-Mg-Sc/Zr, and crack-prone high-strength 2xxx, 6xxx and 7xxx alloys modified with grain refiners. The base design has a Ø25-50 mm build plate on a servo Z piston, a ~6 L vacuum-purgeable argon chamber, a dose-from-above hopper cartridge of ~100 cm3 instead of a supply piston, a servo ball-screw recoater, and a fixed galvanometer scanner above a window in the lid. Please review the peer-reviewed literature (and machine-builder documentation where it is the only source), with citations and quantitative values, on:

1. Heated build plates in LPBF. Preheat temperatures used for aluminium alloys and their effects on cracking, porosity, residual stress, in-situ ageing or over-ageing, and microstructure (AlSi10Mg at 35-200 C and above; Al-Mg-Sc/Zr; crack suppression in 2xxx and 7xxx), and for other alloys (Ti-6Al-4V, Ni superalloys, intermetallics, tungsten) up to 500-1200 C. Heater technologies (resistive cartridge or film heaters, induction, infrared lamps, laser preheating) and the maximum temperatures each reaches. Thermal isolation of a heated plate from the piston, piston seals and Z guides; temperature uniformity and measurement; effects of a hot powder bed on the powder (sintering or caking, Mg and Zn evaporation, oxidation, reuse); and effects of heating on the chamber gas, the lid window and the O2 sensors.
2. Interchangeable build-plate sizes and reduced build volume (RBV) inserts: how research and commercial machines implement them (Renishaw RBV, Aconity, TRUMPF TruPrint 1000 at Ø50 mm, Sisma MYSINT100, EOS M 290 reduced-volume kits, university-built inserts); plate registration, clamping and levelling; piston sealing; powder containment; and whether builds on small plates give microstructures and properties comparable to large plates (thermal mass, heat sinking, part spacing), i.e. how well screening results transfer to production machines.
3. Powder supply variants: interchangeable hopper or cartridge sizes, dose-on-demand feeders (metering roller, vibratory, screw, slot), dosing accuracy and repeatability, powder segregation and residence time in hoppers, multi-material powder delivery, and the minimum powder needed per layer.
4. Automation-friendliness: automated build-plate exchange and removal (zero-point clamping, magnetic or kinematic couplings, build modules or cylinders that leave the machine, Additive Industries MetalFAB, EOS and TRUMPF exchangeable cylinders, robot loading), closed or automated depowdering and powder recovery, sieving, chamber cleaning (condensate and soot removal, cleaning or exchanging the window cover slide), safe handling of reactive condensate, and integration of LPBF into autonomous or self-driving labs (robot arms, gantries, APIs, sensors that confirm each step).

Please end with a ranked list of concrete design choices for a desktop alloy-screening LPBF machine that make the heated plate, the plate size and the hopper size swappable, and make plate removal and chamber cleaning automatable, with the temperature, tolerance and dimension targets the literature supports.

Abstract:
The growing demand for more materials available for the LPBF-process, in particular high-strength aluminum alloys, is evident in the market. In the present work, a systematic investigation of the processability of aluminum 6182 series alloys, using LPBF, was carried out. For this purpose, the influence of process parameters, especially of enhanced preheating by heating the substrate plate during the LPBF process, on the microstructure of EN AW 6182 specimens was studied. Experiments were conducted at different preheating temperatures always using the same d-optimal design-of-experiments, the laser power, scanning speed, hatch distance, and laser focus position being varied over a wide range. It was found that the preheating temperature has the strongest impact on hot cracking. Higher temperatures result in a significantly reduced number of hot cracks in the microstructure. Moreover, an equiaxed microstructure of the specimens manufactured can be observed at preheating temperatures of 500 °C. In addition to the preheating temperature, the achievable part density is most strongly affected by the laser focus position and the laser power, whereas the hatch distance shows no discernible impact on the part density. Furthermore, neither the hatch distance nor the laser focus position shows any significant effect on hot cracking. In combination with the optimal scanning parameters, crack-free parts with a fully equiaxed grain structure and densities > 99.0% can be manufactured via LPBF at a preheating temperature of 500 °C.

By using a second post heating and non-melting laser source with a defocused laser beam and lateral offset, cantilever distortion is reduced more than 7.5%, compared to the reference. Based on pre-tests with 9 different offset parameters, the optimum offset has been identified. Also, an upper limit for the laser power of 65 W is identified for the second heat laser beam with a spot diameter of 380 μm, to avoid re-melting and creating new defects. A theoretical “two bar model,” to explain the residual stress behavior and reduction with multi laser beam offset strategy during the LPBF process, is presented. Furthermore, re-melting cracks, defects, and microstructure are analyzed in conjunction with the second defocused offset laser, in case of a 200 W laser power, an increased scan speed of 1300 mms/s, and a reduced hatch distance. Secondary electron signal (SE) images of re-melting cracks are analyzed and compared to SE-image of hot cracks (solidification cracks). 2024Al is an Al-Cu-Mg series heat-treatable aluminum alloy with high strength and excellent damage resistance. To obtain a high-performance target component of LPBF-formed 2024Al, the effect of process parameters on density, microstructure, and performance is systematically investigated and the thermal cracking phenomenon is analyzed in detail. The results reveal that the optimization of process parameters can suppress the cracks generated during the LPBF forming of 2024Al to a certain extent. When the laser energy density is 741 J/mm3, the maximum density reaches 99.77%, whereas the tensile strength and elongation reach 330 ± 7 MPa and 9 ± 0.6%, respectively. In addition, an extremely high cooling rate (−108 K/s) and heat input during LPBF forming reduce the liquid phase filling rate at grain boundaries to further aggravate the thermal cracking tendency. The current study provides experimental guidance for the preparation of high-quality, crack-less, or even crack-free 2024Al alloys.

One of the main limitations of laser powder bed fusion technology is the residual stress (RS) introduced into the material by the local heating of the laser beam. RS restricts the processability of some materials and causes shape distortions in the process. Powder bed preheating is a commonly used technique for RS mitigation. Therefore, the objective of this study was to investigate the effect of powder bed preheating in the range of room temperature to 400 °C on RS, macrostructure, microstructure, mechanical properties, and properties of the unfused powder of the nickel-based superalloy Inconel 939. The effect of base plate preheating on RS was determined by an indirect method using deformation of the bridge-shaped specimens. Inconel 939 behaved differently than titanium and aluminum alloys when preheated at high temperatures. Preheating at high temperatures resulted in higher RS, higher 0.2% proof stress and ultimate strength, lower elongation at brake, and higher material hardness. The increased RSs and the change in mechanical properties are attributed to changes in the microstructure. Preheating resulted in a larger melt pool, increased the width of columnar grains, and led to evolution of the carbide phase. The most significant microstructure change was in the increase of the size and occurrence of the carbide phase when higher preheating was applied. Furthermore, it was detected that the evolution of the carbide phase strongly corresponds to the build time when high-temperature preheating is applied. Rapid oxidation of the unfused powder was not detected by EDX or XRD analyses.
