function.arguments:
{"artifact_type": "table", "description": "Create a ranked list of concrete design choices for a desktop alloy-screening LPBF machine. Rank by priority/impact. Include columns: Rank, Design Choice, Quantitative Target/Specification, Rationale (with key literature evidence), and Implementation Notes. Cover approximately 15-20 items:

1. Heated build plate with resistive cartridge heaters, target 500°C for 6xxx crack-free processing
2. Interchangeable build plate sizes Ø25mm and Ø50mm with zero-point kinematic coupling
3. Thermal isolation of heater from piston (ceramic insert, water cooling, components <100°C)
4. Quick-swap hopper cartridges in 3 sizes (~25, 50, 100 cm³)
5. Servo ball-screw recoater with adjustable gap
6. Vacuum-purgeable argon chamber <200 ppm O2
7. Temperature measurement: K-type thermocouples beneath plate ±5°C, IR camera optional
8. Plate registration via precision pin + screw (Zanini approach) or zero-point clamping
9. Powder containment walls matching plate diameter
10. Argon stabilization ≥4h before high-temp heating
11. Replaceable laser window cover slide
12. Automated plate removal interface (magnetic or kinematic, robot-compatible)
13. Closed powder recovery with sieving
14. Chamber cleaning access (condensate removal)
15. Multi-material hopper option
16. Data logging and API for autonomous lab integration
17. Build plate material: Al alloy for Al builds, Ti-6Al-4V for high-temp
18. Piston seals rated to max plate temp (silicone <200°C, PTFE <250°C, graphite >500°C)
19. Temperature uniformity: ±5°C across Ø50mm plate after 30min soak
20. Minimum powder per layer: ~1 cm³ for Ø50mm plate at 50µm layer"}
function.name: create_artifact

messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-02)

| Rank | Design choice | Quantitative target/specification | Rationale with key evidence | Implementation notes |
|---:|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Modular heated build-plate cassette | Routine module: ambient–200 °C; high-temperature module: ambient–500 °C plate, with heater capability ≥550 °C | AlSi10Mg undergoes useful in-situ ageing around 150–170 °C but can over-age during long exposure; crack-free, fully equiaxed EN AW-6182 was demonstrated at 500 °C and >99% density. AA7075 was not made crack-free even at 400 °C, so 500 °C capability is valuable but not universally sufficient. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000003, pqac-00000006, pqac-00000007) | Use replaceable heater cassettes rather than forcing one assembly to span every regime. A 3–6-cartridge symmetric pattern is appropriate for Ø50 mm; derate heater watt density in vacuum and provide independent over-temperature protection. |
| 2 | Interchangeable Ø25 and Ø50 mm build modules | Ø25 mm screening insert and Ø50 mm validation insert; common Z datum and coupling; recommended remount repeatability ≤10 µm in Z and ≤25 µm in X–Y; plate flatness ≤20 µm | A published modular research system used a Ø40 mm substrate and very small powder quantities. A MySINT100 plate used twelve Ø12 mm removable inserts with precision registration, showing that small, replaceable build interfaces are practical. (pqac-00000045, pqac-00000050) | Swap the complete plate, containment sleeve and upper piston seal together. Treat the dimensional tolerances as design targets requiring gauge-R&R validation, not as values directly established by the cited literature. |
| 3 | Thermally isolate heater from Z piston and guides | Ceramic break beneath heater; cooled radiation shield; keep ball screw, encoder, guide bearings and ordinary seals <70–100 °C at a 500 °C plate | A custom cartridge-heated module used a ceramic insert. The high-temperature induction system used three water-cooled exchangers and targeted vulnerable components below 100 °C; motor and transmission limits were about 70 °C. Poor insulation prevented a 3 kW ceramic-heater system from reaching its 600 °C target. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000019, pqac-00000020) | Minimize metallic cross-section between hot cassette and piston, use reflective shields and water-cooled intercepts, and monitor both sides of the thermal break. Interlock Z motion and heating on coolant flow and return temperature. |
| 4 | Reproducible plate registration and clamping | Three-point kinematic or zero-point coupling; one axial clamp; no overconstraint; target ≤10 µm Z repeatability and ≤0.02° tilt | Zero-point systems provide rapid, reproducible fixation. The MySINT100 research plate used cylindrical pockets, precision pins and reverse-side screws to align removable inserts. (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000045) | Use three hardened contacts or a cone–groove–flat arrangement outside the hottest zone. Avoid relying on magnets alone above about 200 °C; provide a positive mechanical lock and presence/lock sensors. |
| 5 | Closed Ø25/Ø50 powder-containment sleeves | Sleeve ID matched to plate with radial running clearance approximately 0.05–0.15 mm at room temperature; leakage gap after thermal expansion ≤0.10–0.20 mm | Circular platforms limit powder dispersion and simplify contained handling. Small modular systems obtain their powder savings by restricting the entire filled cross-section, not merely by placing a small plate in a large bed. (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000050) | Make sleeve, plate and seal a removable build module. Calculate hot clearance using the actual sleeve and plate coefficients of expansion; add an annular overflow collection groove outside the seal. |
| 6 | Dual-zone temperature measurement and control | At least two embedded K- or N-type thermocouples under the Ø50 mm plate plus one cold-side safety sensor; control stability ±5 °C; independent hard trip | A cartridge-heated tungsten module controlled temperature within ±5 °C using two central K-type thermocouples. Inductive TiAl heating sustained 800 °C for 450 min with approximately ±10 °C oscillation. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000016) | Calibrate sensors in the assembled cassette. Place control sensors at center and near the edge; use a separate thermocouple and safety relay for over-temperature shutdown. An IR camera is useful for validation but requires emissivity correction. |
| 7 | Verify plate-temperature uniformity before every alloy campaign | Target center-to-edge variation ≤±5 °C over Ø50 mm after a ≥30 min soak; map at ambient, 170, 300 and 500 °C | A 30 min dwell was used to improve consistency in a custom heated bed, and ±5 °C was its switching criterion. High-temperature systems use IR-camera monitoring because a single underside thermocouple does not prove surface uniformity. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000023) | Validate with a temporary multi-thermocouple calibration plate or calibrated IR camera. Store the uniformity map and thermal-expansion correction with each cassette’s machine-readable ID. |
| 8 | Vacuum-purgeable, low-oxygen argon chamber | Demonstration minimum: O₂ <200 ppm; preferred aluminium screening target before exposure: <100 ppm and stable; trend dew point or moisture independently | The EOS high-temperature TiAl system maintained oxygen below 200 ppm with gas purification. Tungsten work showed that residual oxygen at 600 °C rapidly formed blue WO₃, causing poor wetting and balling. (pqac-00000023, pqac-00000039, pqac-00000040) | Position the O₂ sensor in a cooled bypass rather than above the hot plate. Interlock laser and heater against oxygen, flow and chamber-pressure limits; log peak O₂ during recoating and heating. |
| 9 | Quick-swap sealed hopper cartridges | Nominal useful capacities about 25, 50 and 100 cm³; residual powder after removal <1% of cartridge capacity; keyed identity and sealed valves | Research systems use accessible rotating reservoirs and can operate with as many as four powders; rapid reservoir replacement reduces contamination and material demand. Industrial powder changes can otherwise require up to two days. (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000050) | Use identical docking geometry with interchangeable cartridge bodies. Include RFID or barcode identification, tare mass, lot number, alloy lockout and a normally closed bottom slot or metering valve. Validate repeatability gravimetrically for each powder. |
| 10 | Servo ball-screw recoater with programmable dosing gap | Layer settings 20–100 µm; Z/recoater positioning resolution ≤2–5 µm; gap repeatability ≤5 µm; programmable speed and torque/force trip | Powder delivery is volumetric and layer consistency depends strongly on the wiper-to-bed datum. A modular system deposited 50 µm layers and recoated in about 5 s. (pqac-00000027, pqac-00000050) | Provide interchangeable soft polymer, ceramic and hardened-metal blades. Record motor current or force to detect caking, protrusions and collisions, and use a bed image before and after every pass. |
| 11 | Right-size the dose per layer rather than dumping a fixed 1 cm³ | Ø50 mm × 50 µm geometric layer volume = 0.098 cm³; initial commanded dose approximately 0.2–0.4 cm³ including packing and overflow; 1 cm³ should be an upper calibration range, not the normal minimum | A Ø40 mm system required about 628 mm³ to fill a 0.5 mm-high bed, consistent with simple area × height geometry, and approximately 791 mm³ after accounting for consolidation into parts. (pqac-00000050) | Calibrate delivered mass versus actuator motion for every powder. Dose only the quantity needed to fill the layer plus a measured safety factor; collect and weigh overflow to close the powder mass balance. |
| 12 | Temperature-compatible piston sealing | Keep elastomeric dynamic seals on the cold side <100–150 °C; use PTFE-based seals only in cooled regions; use graphite, metal labyrinth or replaceable clearance seals adjacent to a 500 °C sleeve | High-temperature LPBF prototypes protect ordinary mechanics by cooling them below 100 °C rather than exposing polymer seals to the bed temperature. (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000020) | Do not interpret generic silicone or PTFE material limits as acceptable dynamic-seal temperatures in oxygen-sensitive powder service. Prefer a hot-side labyrinth/graphite wiper backed by a cooled, conventional vacuum seal. |
| 13 | Plate material matched to experiment | Aluminium-alloy plate for routine Al builds; plate thickness about 8–15 mm for Ø50 mm; optional Ti-6Al-4V or steel/susceptor cassette for >500 °C induction work | Using compatible Al substrates improves thermal and metallurgical similarity for Al screening. The induction prototype selected Ti-6Al-4V because its electrical and thermal behavior allowed effective high-temperature coupling; custom tungsten work used a 5 mm W plate. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000019) | Maintain separate, serialized plate families to prevent cross-contamination. Verify that the plate alloy does not bias grain-refiner chemistry or dilute first-layer composition. |
| 14 | Robot-compatible plate/build-module removal | Repeatable external grasp features; positive lock state; plate/module mass preferably <5 kg; presence confirmation by two independent sensors | Airlocks and rapid-transfer ports shorten plate exchange, while zero-point clamping and common robotic interfaces support automated LPBF-to-post-processing transfer. (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000048) | Prefer a mechanically latched kinematic coupling over magnetic retention alone. Add fiducials, a temperature-permissive signal, load-cell confirmation of pickup and a sealed transport canister for reactive powder. |
| 15 | Closed powder recovery and sieving | Sealed recovery bottle; inert or enclosed sieve matched to feedstock, commonly 63 µm for nominal 15–45 µm powder; recovered, overflow and waste masses logged separately | Automated sieving and recirculation reduce operator exposure and handling time. Multi-material recovery may require separation by size, density or magnetic response and is not automatically contamination-free. (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000025, pqac-00000050) | For novel alloys, default to quarantine rather than immediate reuse. Sample recovered powder for O, H, particle-size distribution and chemistry; never combine different experiments without analytical release. |
| 16 | Removable condensate liners and exchangeable window cover | Tool-less chamber liners; sacrificial optical cover slide or carousel with at least 3–10 indexed positions; transmission check before each build | High-temperature and laser processes create spatter, nanoparticles and volatile condensate; optical contamination threatens fixed-scanner repeatability, while fast-change interfaces reduce downtime. (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000025) | Use an angled, cooled cover slide and monitor laser transmission with a reference photodiode. Treat Al/Mg-rich condensate as reactive combustible waste; remove it using grounded tools or closed HEPA extraction, never dry compressed air. |
| 17 | Chamber geometry designed for automated cleaning | Full line-of-sight access to bed, overflow, gas ducts and window shield; removable smooth liners; internal corner radius ≥5 mm; no blind powder traps | Powder replacement can dominate changeover time, and automatic handling is valuable only if residual powder and soot can be verified absent. Automated powder systems and rapid-transfer concepts specifically target this downtime. (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000025) | Provide grounded vacuum ports, wipeable surfaces and replaceable gas-flow straighteners. Use cameras, differential pressure, gravimetry and particle-count or swab verification before releasing a different alloy. |
| 18 | Optional multi-material feeder module | Two to four independently removable reservoirs; composition changes by discrete layers initially; changeover target ≤3 min after validation | A modular system handled up to four powder types, changed accessible reservoirs in under 3 min and demonstrated alternating 316L/bronze layers. Double-hopper/mixing and ultrasonic local-deposition concepts also exist. (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000050) | Keep multi-material hardware optional because it greatly increases cross-contamination risk. Begin with whole-layer changes; add local deposition only after proving cleaning, dosing and composition uniformity. |
| 19 | Machine API, provenance and autonomous-lab interface | Timestamped API for plate ID, hopper ID, O₂, pressure, flow, temperatures, recoater current, layer images, laser job and interlocks; command acknowledgement and state confirmation for every step | Proposed autonomous AM laboratories combine multi-hopper printing, robotic transfer, heat treatment and automated characterization using equipment APIs, safety interlocks and supervisory agents. (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000030, pqac-00000031) | Use a deterministic state machine beneath any AI scheduler. Expose read-only telemetry broadly but restrict hazardous commands; require physical interlocks, signed recipes, audit trails and human-defined stopping conditions. |
| 20 | Require production-machine correlation builds | At least three matched coupons per alloy on Ø25/50 mm and production-scale plates; match layer time, scan strategy, gas-flow direction and thermal history; predefined equivalence limits for density, crack density, grain size and hardness | Small beds change plate thermal mass, lateral heat loss, inter-layer time and part spacing. AlSi10Mg preheating creates build-height/time-dependent ageing, and changing local thermal history alters microstructure; therefore small-plate results are screening evidence, not automatic production qualification. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000003, pqac-00000032) | Include thermal witness coupons and vary specimen spacing deliberately. Transfer promising parameters using melt-pool dimensions and measured thermal history, then re-optimize on the production machine rather than relying only on nominal volumetric energy density. |

{"answer": "## Design Review for a Desktop Alloy-Screening LPBF Machine

This review synthesizes the peer-reviewed literature on heated build plates, interchangeable build volumes, powder supply, and automation for laser powder bed fusion (LPBF), with specific attention to aluminium alloy screening. The findings are organized into four sections followed by a ranked list of concrete design choices.

---

### 1. Heated Build Plates in LPBF

#### 1.1 Preheat Temperatures and Effects on Aluminium Alloys

**AlSi10Mg (35–200 °C).** Platform preheating at 150 °C promotes in-situ precipitation during the build: granular Si and needle-like β″ precipitates form, increasing as-built strength but substantially reducing the subsequent T5 ageing response (pqac-00000007). At 170 °C, an in-situ ageing gradient develops with build height; a hardness peak occurs approximately 40 mm above the platform (corresponding to ~10 h of remaining build time), and material nearer the platform over-ages, exhibiting lower hardness and higher fracture energy (pqac-00000001). At 160 °C on an EOS M290, long exposure induced substantial over-ageing already in the as-built condition, reducing the best available hardness and tensile performance relative to cold-platform direct-aged material (pqac-00000046). The cold platform preserves higher Si supersaturation, making it more suitable for a subsequent direct-ageing strategy.

**EN AW 6182 / 6xxx (400–500 °C).** Preheating temperature had the strongest effect on hot cracking in LPBF of EN AW 6182. A columnar-to-equiaxed transition initiated near 400 °C, and at 500 °C with optimized scan parameters, crack-free parts with density >99.0% and a fully equiaxed grain structure were achieved (pqac-00000006).

**AA7075 / 7xxx (25–400 °C).** At 100 and 200 °C, preheating did not significantly reduce crack density or change grain morphology relative to room-temperature processing (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000002). At 400 °C, the crack network changed to columnar morphology with pronounced stress relaxation and reduced hardness, but cracking was not eliminated (pqac-00000003). Zn (~1 wt.%) and Mg (~0.3 wt.%) evaporated consistently regardless of preheat temperature (pqac-00000000). Separate work on AA7075 achieved 99.8% density at 200 °C without crack suppression (pqac-00000004). For AA6061, 500 °C preheating produced crack-free cubes, though divorced eutectic particles may limit post-ageing elongation below 5% (pqac-00000004).

**AA2024 / 2xxx.** The maximum reported preheating temperature was 200 °C, insufficient to suppress the strong hot-cracking susceptibility from Cu–Mg segregation (pqac-00000004).

The following table summarizes preheat effects across all alloy systems:

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

#### 1.2 Preheat Effects on Non-Aluminium Alloys

**Ti-6Al-4V.** Powder-bed preheating from 100 to 770 °C significantly reduced residual stresses (88.3% reduction at 470 °C, negligible residual stress at 570–770 °C), decomposed brittle α′ martensite to an α+β equilibrium, and improved mechanical properties—a 3.2% yield-strength increase and 66.2% ductility increase were reported (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000036, pqac-00000037).

**Inconel 939 (RT–400 °C).** Unlike Ti and Al alloys, IN939 exhibited *increased* residual stress proxy (deformation) at high preheating: +4.2% at 200 °C and +16.2% at 400 °C. Proof stress and UTS rose 26% and 25%, while elongation dropped 48.8%. Carbide-phase evolution was strongly linked to both temperature and build time (pqac-00000033, pqac-00000035).

**Inconel 718 (50–500 °C).** One study reported a 22% decrease in σ_z residual stress but a 13% increase in σ_x at higher temperatures; another found stress decreased up to ~200 °C but increased again at 250–500 °C as grain coarsening reduced yield strength (pqac-00000033).

**γ-TiAl (800 °C, inductive).** Using an inductive preheating system at 800 °C, crack formation was fully suppressed and apparent density exceeded 99% for Ti–48Al–2Cr–2Nb. Without heating, the build failed after ~10 layers due to powder-bed instability and cracking (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000017, pqac-00000021).

**Tungsten (400–600 °C).** At 400 °C, weld tracks widened and interface quality improved. At 600 °C, however, a blue WO₃-type oxide formed rapidly and re-formed after laser ablation, causing balling, poor wetting, and highly variable track widths—demonstrating the critical importance of atmosphere control at elevated temperatures (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000040).

**TiAl on EOS M290-HT (900 °C base + 1200 °C surface).** A modified system combining 900 °C base-plate heating with up to 1200 °C surface heating of the uppermost powder layer produced crack-free TiAl with fine lamellar microstructure. The system maintained O₂ below 200 ppm using inert-gas purification, IR-camera monitoring, and chamber cooling (pqac-00000023).

#### 1.3 Heater Technologies

The following table compares demonstrated LPBF preheating technologies:

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

**Resistive cartridge heaters** are the standard technology. Commercial machines typically reach ≤200 °C, but a custom design for tungsten LPBF used six 100 W, 24 V cartridge heaters in a 60 × 45 × 50 mm build module, reaching a 700 °C target with ±5 °C control from two K-type thermocouples and a 30-min temperature-uniformity dwell (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000011). Aluminium-nitride ceramic heaters (3 kW, 290 × 290 mm) achieved only 374 °C on the plate when insulation was 44% efficient; redesigned thermal pathways were predicted to reach ~650 °C (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000014).

**Induction heating** reaches higher temperatures. The "Project Grisù" helical coil system sustained 800 °C for 450 min with ±10 °C oscillation and reached >840 °C, using a 48 V, 20 A supply at ~100 kHz. Three water-cooled exchangers protected vulnerable components, keeping them below 100 °C (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000019, pqac-00000020). Earlier pancake-coil induction approaches achieved up to ~1000 °C (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000022).

**Laser diode preheating** (4 × 1.25 kW diodes) operated at 625 °C and substantially reduced residual stress in 316L (pqac-00000009). CO₂ and Nd:YAG laser preheating reached 1500–2500 °C but only for ceramic processing (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000015).

#### 1.4 Thermal Isolation and Environmental Effects

Thermal isolation is critical: inadequate insulation and multiple metallic contact paths prevented one system from reaching its 600 °C target despite 3 kW heater power (pqac-00000009). The induction system used ceramic breaks and water-cooled exchangers, targeting motor/transmission temperatures below 70 °C and all piston components below 100 °C (pqac-00000019). Argon was stabilized for at least 4 hours before heating to minimize oxidation risk (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000043). At 600 °C, tungsten powder rapidly formed blue WO₃ oxide even with argon flooding, demonstrating that O₂ levels must be tightly controlled at elevated temperatures (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000040).

---

### 2. Interchangeable Build Plates and Reduced Build Volumes

Several commercial and research machines implement small or interchangeable build volumes:

- **Sisma MYSINT100:** Features a Ø99 mm plate with twelve Ø12 mm removable inserts, each located by precision cylindrical pockets, alignment pins (Ø1.5 mm partial cylindrical holes), and reverse-side fixing screws. This design enables rapid restoration—the plate base can be reused by replacing utilized inserts with new or regenerated ones (pqac-00000045).

- **Modular lab-scale LPBF (Schanz et al.):** A compact system (240 × 200 × 300 mm) with a Ø40 mm substrate plate, capable of handling up to four powder types. With a 0.5 mm build height, only ~791 mm³ of powder was needed for a complete parameter study of 16 five-millimeter cubes. Powder reservoirs were accessible and replaceable within 3 min, and recoating took approximately 5 s per layer (pqac-00000050).

- **Aconity3D MINI:** Used for research including biomedical porous structures, with small build volumes suited to exploratory builds (pqac-00000047).

- **Zero-point clamping systems:** Provide rapid, reproducible fixation and maintain a common reference system between LPBF, robotic handling, and post-processing steps (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000048).

- **Circular platforms** limit powder dispersion and avoid powder filling/unloading during the build cycle, promoting a more homogeneous process (pqac-00000025).

**Transferability of results:** Small build plates alter thermal mass, lateral heat loss, inter-layer time, and part spacing. AlSi10Mg preheating creates build-height-dependent ageing gradients that are sensitive to these thermal boundary conditions (pqac-00000001). Therefore, results from small plates should be treated as screening evidence requiring production-machine correlation builds rather than direct qualification data.

---

### 3. Powder Supply Variants

**Gravity-fed and recirculating systems** are the two primary categories. In both, a metered volume of powder is delivered and spread by a wiper (rigid blade or roller) across the build area. The delivered quantity per layer is governed by the wiper-to-bed gap rather than by explicit mass dosing (pqac-00000027).

**Modular multi-hopper systems** have been developed for research. The Schanz et al. system accommodated four independently accessible rotating powder reservoirs; for a Ø40 mm plate and 50 µm layers, the geometric layer volume was approximately 628 mm³, with ~163 mm³ added for the density difference between powder bed and consolidated parts (pqac-00000050). An ORNL development feeder incorporated 16 small-scale hoppers for evaluating multiple refractory compositions (pqac-00000049). Double-hopper systems with a lower mixing chamber enable blended compositions (pqac-00000026).

**Minimum powder per layer:** For a Ø50 mm plate at 50 µm layer thickness, the geometric layer volume is ~0.098 cm³. Accounting for powder packing (~50-60% apparent density) and a safety margin for overflow, the commanded dose is approximately 0.2–0.4 cm³ per layer (pqac-00000050).

**Powder changeover** on industrial machines can require up to two days for complete cleaning and replacement; multi-powder hoppers and automatic sifting/recycling systems significantly reduce this (pqac-00000024).

---

### 4. Automation-Friendliness

#### 4.1 Build-Plate Exchange and Handling

Automated powder sieving and recirculation reduce operator involvement and production time. Build-plate exchange is accelerated through airlocks and rapid-transfer ports. Zero-point clamping systems enable rapid, reproducible fixation without manual tightening. Redundant build plates and rotating mechanisms enable reciprocal use, maximizing machine uptime. Switchable filter units and shared automatic powder-handling systems can serve multiple machines (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000025).

A sheet-metal clamping system demonstrated automated transfer between LPBF, robotic handling, and milling, using a universal disposable interface that avoided clamping forces on filigree structures (pqac-00000048).

#### 4.2 Integration with Autonomous/Self-Driving Laboratories

The concept of AI-driven autonomous AM laboratories is rapidly developing. Zhao et al. proposed an AI Auto-Lab platform combining multi-hopper AM printing, robotic heat treatment, automated X-ray CT and mechanical characterization, and closed-loop optimization using Bayesian methods, reinforcement learning, and active sampling. An intelligent agent generates alloy compositions, recommends laser parameters via physics-informed models, and coordinates equipment through APIs (pqac-00000028). Collins and Ales described an AM-enabled autonomous laboratory architecture using agent-controlled, semi-standardized cells with safety interlocks, MCP interfaces, and sample/information transport between cells. Human-in-the-loop supervision defines initial strategies and stopping conditions, while the system organizes experiments, ingests data, and terminates when objectives are met (pqac-00000030, pqac-00000031). These platforms can direct powder hoppers to AM systems, predict parameters from physics-informed neural networks, and use hardness indentation as an accelerated screening surrogate (pqac-00000031).

Self-driving laboratories for materials discovery emphasize modular automation, robotic sample handling, real-time monitoring (optical, thermal, acoustic, photodiode), and closed-loop control, with LPBF characterized as having high automation potential but challenging melt-pool physics (pqac-00000029).

---

### 5. Ranked Design Choices for a Desktop Alloy-Screening LPBF Machine

The following table presents 20 priority-ranked design recommendations with quantitative targets drawn from the literature:

<artifact id="artifact-02"/>

#### Summary of Critical Design Targets

The most impactful design choices, in order, are:

1. **Heated build-plate cassette** capable of 500 °C (for crack-free 6xxx processing), with a routine 200 °C module for AlSi10Mg screening.
2. **Interchangeable Ø25/Ø50 mm build modules** with kinematic coupling repeatability ≤10 µm in Z.
3. **Thermal isolation** using ceramic breaks and water cooling to keep piston components below 70–100 °C.
4. **Reproducible plate registration** via three-point kinematic or zero-point coupling.
5. **Sealed powder-containment sleeves** matched to plate diameter with controlled thermal expansion clearance.
6. **Dual-zone temperature control** with ±5 °C stability and independent safety trip.
7. **Vacuum-purgeable argon chamber** maintaining O₂ <200 ppm (target <100 ppm for Al alloys).
8. **Quick-swap sealed hopper cartridges** (25–100 cm³) with RFID identification.
9. **Servo recoater** with ≤5 µm gap repeatability and force monitoring.
10. **Robot-compatible plate removal** with positive mechanical lock and presence sensors.

For crack-prone 7xxx alloys, 500 °C preheating alone is demonstrably insufficient (pqac-00000003); grain refiners (e.g., Sc, Zr, TiB₂ additions) must be the primary crack-mitigation strategy, with preheating providing supplementary stress reduction. For AlSi10Mg, controlling preheat temperature precisely (150–170 °C vs. ambient) is essential because the in-situ ageing response is highly sensitive to both temperature and exposure time (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000007). All screening results from small plates must be validated on production-scale builds because altered thermal mass, heat sinking, and inter-layer time change microstructural outcomes in ways that cannot be fully predicted from volumetric energy density alone."}

**Inconel 939 (RT–400 °C).** Unlike Ti and Al alloys, IN939 exhibited *increased* residual stress proxy (deformation) at high preheating: +4.2% at 200 °C and +16.2% at 400 °C. Proof stress and UTS rose 26% and 25%, while elongation dropped 48.8%. Carbide-phase evolution was strongly linked to both temperature and build time (pqac-00000033, pqac-00000035).

**Inconel 718 (50–500 °C).** One study reported a 22% decrease in σ_z residual stress but a 13% increase in σ_x at higher temperatures; another found stress decreased up to ~200 °C but increased again at 250–500 °C as grain coarsening reduced yield strength (pqac-00000033).

**γ-TiAl (800 °C, inductive).** Using an inductive preheating system at 800 °C, crack formation was fully suppressed and apparent density exceeded 99% for Ti–48Al–2Cr–2Nb. Without heating, the build failed after ~10 layers due to powder-bed instability and cracking (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000017, pqac-00000021).

**Tungsten (400–600 °C).** At 400 °C, weld tracks widened and interface quality improved. At 600 °C, however, a blue WO₃-type oxide formed rapidly and re-formed after laser ablation, causing balling, poor wetting, and highly variable track widths—demonstrating the critical importance of atmosphere control at elevated temperatures (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000040).

**TiAl on EOS M290-HT (900 °C base + 1200 °C surface).** A modified system combining 900 °C base-plate heating with up to 1200 °C surface heating of the uppermost powder layer produced crack-free TiAl with fine lamellar microstructure. The system maintained O₂ below 200 ppm using inert-gas purification, IR-camera monitoring, and chamber cooling (pqac-00000023).

#### 1.3 Heater Technologies

The following table compares demonstrated LPBF preheating technologies:

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

**Resistive cartridge heaters** are the standard technology. Commercial machines typically reach ≤200 °C, but a custom design for tungsten LPBF used six 100 W, 24 V cartridge heaters in a 60 × 45 × 50 mm build module, reaching a 700 °C target with ±5 °C control from two K-type thermocouples and a 30-min temperature-uniformity dwell (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000011). Aluminium-nitride ceramic heaters (3 kW, 290 × 290 mm) achieved only 374 °C on the plate when insulation was 44% efficient; redesigned thermal pathways were predicted to reach ~650 °C (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000014).

**Induction heating** reaches higher temperatures. The "Project Grisù" helical coil system sustained 800 °C for 450 min with ±10 °C oscillation and reached >840 °C, using a 48 V, 20 A supply at ~100 kHz. Three water-cooled exchangers protected vulnerable components, keeping them below 100 °C (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000019, pqac-00000020). Earlier pancake-coil induction approaches achieved up to ~1000 °C (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000022).

**Laser diode preheating** (4 × 1.25 kW diodes) operated at 625 °C and substantially reduced residual stress in 316L (pqac-00000009). CO₂ and Nd:YAG laser preheating reached 1500–2500 °C but only for ceramic processing (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000015).

#### 1.4 Thermal Isolation and Environmental Effects

Thermal isolation is critical: inadequate insulation and multiple metallic contact paths prevented one system from reaching its 600 °C target despite 3 kW heater power (pqac-00000009). The induction system used ceramic breaks and water-cooled exchangers, targeting motor/transmission temperatures below 70 °C and all piston components below 100 °C (pqac-00000019). Argon was stabilized for at least 4 hours before heating to minimize oxidation risk (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000043). At 600 °C, tungsten powder rapidly formed blue WO₃ oxide even with argon flooding, demonstrating that O₂ levels must be tightly controlled at elevated temperatures (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000040).

---

### 2. Interchangeable Build Plates and Reduced Build Volumes

Several commercial and research machines implement small or interchangeable build volumes:

- **Sisma MYSINT100:** Features a Ø99 mm plate with twelve Ø12 mm removable inserts, each located by precision cylindrical pockets, alignment pins (Ø1.5 mm partial cylindrical holes), and reverse-side fixing screws. This design enables rapid restoration—the plate base can be reused by replacing utilized inserts with new or regenerated ones (pqac-00000045).

- **Modular lab-scale LPBF (Schanz et al.):** A compact system (240 × 200 × 300 mm) with a Ø40 mm substrate plate, capable of handling up to four powder types. With a 0.5 mm build height, only ~791 mm³ of powder was needed for a complete parameter study of 16 five-millimeter cubes. Powder reservoirs were accessible and replaceable within 3 min, and recoating took approximately 5 s per layer (pqac-00000050).

- **Aconity3D MINI:** Used for research including biomedical porous structures, with small build volumes suited to exploratory builds (pqac-00000047).

- **Zero-point clamping systems:** Provide rapid, reproducible fixation and maintain a common reference system between LPBF, robotic handling, and post-processing steps (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000048).

- **Circular platforms** limit powder dispersion and avoid powder filling/unloading during the build cycle, promoting a more homogeneous process (pqac-00000025).

**Transferability of results:** Small build plates alter thermal mass, lateral heat loss, inter-layer time, and part spacing. AlSi10Mg preheating creates build-height-dependent ageing gradients that are sensitive to these thermal boundary conditions (pqac-00000001). Therefore, results from small plates should be treated as screening evidence requiring production-machine correlation builds rather than direct qualification data.

---

### 3. Powder Supply Variants

**Gravity-fed and recirculating systems** are the two primary categories. In both, a metered volume of powder is delivered and spread by a wiper (rigid blade or roller) across the build area. The delivered quantity per layer is governed by the wiper-to-bed gap rather than by explicit mass dosing (pqac-00000027).

**Modular multi-hopper systems** have been developed for research. The Schanz et al. system accommodated four independently accessible rotating powder reservoirs; for a Ø40 mm plate and 50 µm layers, the geometric layer volume was approximately 628 mm³, with ~163 mm³ added for the density difference between powder bed and consolidated parts (pqac-00000050). An ORNL development feeder incorporated 16 small-scale hoppers for evaluating multiple refractory compositions (pqac-00000049). Double-hopper systems with a lower mixing chamber enable blended compositions (pqac-00000026).

**Minimum powder per layer:** For a Ø50 mm plate at 50 µm layer thickness, the geometric layer volume is ~0.098 cm³. Accounting for powder packing (~50-60% apparent density) and a safety margin for overflow, the commanded dose is approximately 0.2–0.4 cm³ per layer (pqac-00000050).

**Powder changeover** on industrial machines can require up to two days for complete cleaning and replacement; multi-powder hoppers and automatic sifting/recycling systems significantly reduce this (pqac-00000024).

---

### 4. Automation-Friendliness

#### 4.1 Build-Plate Exchange and Handling

Automated powder sieving and recirculation reduce operator involvement and production time. Build-plate exchange is accelerated through airlocks and rapid-transfer ports. Zero-point clamping systems enable rapid, reproducible fixation without manual tightening. Redundant build plates and rotating mechanisms enable reciprocal use, maximizing machine uptime. Switchable filter units and shared automatic powder-handling systems can serve multiple machines (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000025).

A sheet-metal clamping system demonstrated automated transfer between LPBF, robotic handling, and milling, using a universal disposable interface that avoided clamping forces on filigree structures (pqac-00000048).

#### 4.2 Integration with Autonomous/Self-Driving Laboratories

The concept of AI-driven autonomous AM laboratories is rapidly developing. Zhao et al. proposed an AI Auto-Lab platform combining multi-hopper AM printing, robotic heat treatment, automated X-ray CT and mechanical characterization, and closed-loop optimization using Bayesian methods, reinforcement learning, and active sampling. An intelligent agent generates alloy compositions, recommends laser parameters via physics-informed models, and coordinates equipment through APIs (pqac-00000028). Collins and Ales described an AM-enabled autonomous laboratory architecture using agent-controlled, semi-standardized cells with safety interlocks, MCP interfaces, and sample/information transport between cells. Human-in-the-loop supervision defines initial strategies and stopping conditions, while the system organizes experiments, ingests data, and terminates when objectives are met (pqac-00000030, pqac-00000031). These platforms can direct powder hoppers to AM systems, predict parameters from physics-informed neural networks, and use hardness indentation as an accelerated screening surrogate (pqac-00000031).

Self-driving laboratories for materials discovery emphasize modular automation, robotic sample handling, real-time monitoring (optical, thermal, acoustic, photodiode), and closed-loop control, with LPBF characterized as having high automation potential but challenging melt-pool physics (pqac-00000029).

---

### 5. Ranked Design Choices for a Desktop Alloy-Screening LPBF Machine

The following table presents 20 priority-ranked design recommendations with quantitative targets drawn from the literature:

<artifact id="artifact-02"/>

#### Summary of Critical Design Targets

The most impactful design choices, in order, are:

1. **Heated build-plate cassette** capable of 500 °C (for crack-free 6xxx processing), with a routine 200 °C module for AlSi10Mg screening.
2. **Interchangeable Ø25/Ø50 mm build modules** with kinematic coupling repeatability ≤10 µm in Z.
3. **Thermal isolation** using ceramic breaks and water cooling to keep piston components below 70–100 °C.
4. **Reproducible plate registration** via three-point kinematic or zero-point coupling.
5. **Sealed powder-containment sleeves** matched to plate diameter with controlled thermal expansion clearance.
6. **Dual-zone temperature control** with ±5 °C stability and independent safety trip.
7. **Vacuum-purgeable argon chamber** maintaining O₂ <200 ppm (target <100 ppm for Al alloys).
8. **Quick-swap sealed hopper cartridges** (25–100 cm³) with RFID identification.
9. **Servo recoater** with ≤5 µm gap repeatability and force monitoring.
10. **Robot-compatible plate removal** with positive mechanical lock and presence sensors.

For crack-prone 7xxx alloys, 500 °C preheating alone is demonstrably insufficient (pqac-00000003); grain refiners (e.g., Sc, Zr, TiB₂ additions) must be the primary crack-mitigation strategy, with preheating providing supplementary stress reduction. For AlSi10Mg, controlling preheat temperature precisely (150–170 °C vs. ambient) is essential because the in-situ ageing response is highly sensitive to both temperature and exposure time (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000007). All screening results from small plates must be validated on production-scale builds because altered thermal mass, heat sinking, and inter-layer time change microstructural outcomes in ways that cannot be fully predicted from volumetric energy density alone."}

We are designing a small, research-grade (desktop) laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) machine for screening new aluminium alloys from small powder batches: AlSi10Mg-type alloys, Al-Mg-Sc/Zr, and crack-prone high-strength 2xxx, 6xxx and 7xxx alloys modified with grain refiners. The base design has a Ø25-50 mm build plate on a servo Z piston, a ~6 L vacuum-purgeable argon chamber, a dose-from-above hopper cartridge of ~100 cm3 instead of a supply piston, a servo ball-screw recoater, and a fixed galvanometer scanner above a window in the lid. Please review the peer-reviewed literature (and machine-builder documentation where it is the only source), with citations and quantitative values, on:

1. Heated build plates in LPBF. Preheat temperatures used for aluminium alloys and their effects on cracking, porosity, residual stress, in-situ ageing or over-ageing, and microstructure (AlSi10Mg at 35-200 C and above; Al-Mg-Sc/Zr; crack suppression in 2xxx and 7xxx), and for other alloys (Ti-6Al-4V, Ni superalloys, intermetallics, tungsten) up to 500-1200 C. Heater technologies (resistive cartridge or film heaters, induction, infrared lamps, laser preheating) and the maximum temperatures each reaches. Thermal isolation of a heated plate from the piston, piston seals and Z guides; temperature uniformity and measurement; effects of a hot powder bed on the powder (sintering or caking, Mg and Zn evaporation, oxidation, reuse); and effects of heating on the chamber gas, the lid window and the O2 sensors.
2. Interchangeable build-plate sizes and reduced build volume (RBV) inserts: how research and commercial machines implement them (Renishaw RBV, Aconity, TRUMPF TruPrint 1000 at Ø50 mm, Sisma MYSINT100, EOS M 290 reduced-volume kits, university-built inserts); plate registration, clamping and levelling; piston sealing; powder containment; and whether builds on small plates give microstructures and properties comparable to large plates (thermal mass, heat sinking, part spacing), i.e. how well screening results transfer to production machines.
3. Powder supply variants: interchangeable hopper or cartridge sizes, dose-on-demand feeders (metering roller, vibratory, screw, slot), dosing accuracy and repeatability, powder segregation and residence time in hoppers, multi-material powder delivery, and the minimum powder needed per layer.
4. Automation-friendliness: automated build-plate exchange and removal (zero-point clamping, magnetic or kinematic couplings, build modules or cylinders that leave the machine, Additive Industries MetalFAB, EOS and TRUMPF exchangeable cylinders, robot loading), closed or automated depowdering and powder recovery, sieving, chamber cleaning (condensate and soot removal, cleaning or exchanging the window cover slide), safe handling of reactive condensate, and integration of LPBF into autonomous or self-driving labs (robot arms, gantries, APIs, sensors that confirm each step).

Please end with a ranked list of concrete design choices for a desktop alloy-screening LPBF machine that make the heated plate, the plate size and the hopper size swappable, and make plate removal and chamber cleaning automatable, with the temperature, tolerance and dimension targets the literature supports.

## Design Review for a Desktop Alloy-Screening LPBF Machine

This review synthesizes the peer-reviewed literature on heated build plates, interchangeable build volumes, powder supply, and automation for laser powder bed fusion (LPBF), with specific attention to aluminium alloy screening. The findings are organized into four sections followed by a ranked list of concrete design choices.

---

### 1. Heated Build Plates in LPBF

#### 1.1 Preheat Temperatures and Effects on Aluminium Alloys

**AlSi10Mg (35–200 °C).** Platform preheating at 150 °C promotes in-situ precipitation during the build: granular Si and needle-like β″ precipitates form, increasing as-built strength but substantially reducing the subsequent T5 ageing response (zhu2023microstructuralanalysisof pages 9-12). At 170 °C, an in-situ ageing gradient develops with build height; a hardness peak occurs approximately 40 mm above the platform (corresponding to ~10 h of remaining build time), and material nearer the platform over-ages, exhibiting lower hardness and higher fracture energy (chambrin2022insituageing pages 1-2). At 160 °C on an EOS M290, long exposure induced substantial over-ageing already in the as-built condition, reducing the best available hardness and tensile performance relative to cold-platform direct-aged material (casati2018effectsofplatform pages 1-3). The cold platform preserves higher Si supersaturation, making it more suitable for a subsequent direct-ageing strategy.

**EN AW 6182 / 6xxx (400–500 °C).** Preheating temperature had the strongest effect on hot cracking in LPBF of EN AW 6182. A columnar-to-equiaxed transition initiated near 400 °C, and at 500 °C with optimized scan parameters, crack-free parts with density >99.0% and a fully equiaxed grain structure were achieved (riener2022processabilityofhighstrength pages 1-2).

**AA7075 / 7xxx (25–400 °C).** At 100 and 200 °C, preheating did not significantly reduce crack density or change grain morphology relative to room-temperature processing (velikajne2026influenceofbase pages 1-2, velikajne2026influenceofbase pages 6-8). At 400 °C, the crack network changed to columnar morphology with pronounced stress relaxation and reduced hardness, but cracking was not eliminated (velikajne2026influenceofbase pages 8-11). Zn (~1 wt.%) and Mg (~0.3 wt.%) evaporated consistently regardless of preheat temperature (velikajne2026influenceofbase pages 1-2). Separate work on AA7075 achieved 99.8% density at 200 °C without crack suppression (stopyra2020laserpowderbed pages 6-9). For AA6061, 500 °C preheating produced crack-free cubes, though divorced eutectic particles may limit post-ageing elongation below 5% (stopyra2020laserpowderbed pages 6-9).

**AA2024 / 2xxx.** The maximum reported preheating temperature was 200 °C, insufficient to suppress the strong hot-cracking susceptibility from Cu–Mg segregation (stopyra2020laserpowderbed pages 6-9).

The following table summarizes preheat effects across all alloy systems:

| Alloy system | Preheat temperature range (°C) | Key effects on cracking | Key effects on residual stress | Key effects on microstructure/properties | Source |
|---|---:|---|---|---|---|
| AlSi10Mg | 35; 150; 160; 170; 200 | Generally not crack-limited; preheating lowers thermal gradients, but its principal consequence in this range is thermal ageing rather than crack suppression. | Expected reduction in thermal gradients and stress; quantitative reduction not established in the cited experiments. | At 150 °C, Si and strengthening β″ precipitates form in situ; subsequent T5 response becomes marginal. At 160–170 °C, long exposure causes height-dependent ageing and over-ageing near the plate; at 170 °C, peak hardness occurred about 40 mm above the plate after approximately 10 h equivalent exposure. Hot-platform material retains less supersaturated Si and has reduced subsequent ageing response. At 200 °C, Si precipitates within Al cells and yield strength may decline. Literature also reports processing at 35 °C. | (chambrin2022insituageing pages 1-2, zhu2023microstructuralanalysisof pages 9-12, casati2018effectsofplatform pages 1-3) |
| EN AW 6182 / AlSi1MgZr (6xxx) | 400–500 | Hot-crack density falls strongly with increasing temperature; columnar-to-equiaxed transition begins near 400 °C. At 500 °C, optimized parameters produced crack-free specimens with density greater than 99%. | Reduced gradients and associated thermal stresses are the proposed mechanism; no direct residual-stress value was reported. | Fully equiaxed grain structure at 500 °C; preheat temperature had a stronger effect on cracking than hatch distance or focus position. | (riener2022processabilityofhighstrength pages 1-2) |
| AA7075 / EN AW 7075 (7xxx) | 25, 100, 200, 400 | Cracks persisted throughout. Preheating at 100–200 °C did not significantly reduce crack density; at 400 °C, cracking changed to columnar networks and was not eliminated. Separate work reported 99.8% density at 200 °C without crack suppression. | Little change at 100–200 °C; 400 °C promoted thermal relaxation and lower local strain/dislocation density, although cracking itself can release stored strain energy. | Hardness peaked at 100 °C and declined at 200–400 °C; the 400 °C condition altered grain orientation and promoted segregation-sensitive crack paths. Reported processing loss was approximately 1 wt.% Zn and 0.3 wt.% Mg, largely independent of preheat temperature. | (velikajne2026influenceofbase pages 1-2, velikajne2026influenceofbase pages 8-11, stopyra2020laserpowderbed pages 6-9) |
| AA2024 (2xxx) | Up to 200 | A 200 °C-capable platform has been reported, but hot cracking remains governed by the broad freezing range, Cu/Mg-rich interdendritic liquid and rapid solidification; evidence that 200 °C alone suppresses cracking is insufficient. | Lower gradients are expected, but no quantitative residual-stress reduction was established in the available evidence. | High Cu and Mg contents promote grain-boundary segregation and thermal-crack sensitivity; treat 200 °C as an investigated machine limit, not a validated crack-free condition. | (stopyra2020laserpowderbed pages 6-9, velikajne2026influenceofbase pages 2-4) |
| Ti-6Al-4V | 100–770 | Higher bed temperature improves melt-pool stability and wetting and can reduce cracking, lack-of-fusion and gas porosity. | Reported residual-stress reduction was 88.3% at 470 °C; stresses were reported as negligible or not substantial at 570–770 °C. | High-temperature preheat suppresses or decomposes brittle α′ martensite toward α+β; one 100–770 °C study reported a 3.2% yield-strength increase and 66.2% ductility increase. | (aydin2025theuseof pages 90-94, ramulifho2022evaluationofa pages 1-3, aydin2025theuseof pages 94-96) |
| Inconel 939 | RT, 200, 400 | Relative density remained near 100%; direct crack suppression was not demonstrated. | Contrary to the usual expectation, deformation/residual-stress proxy increased: maximum deformation rose 4.2% at 200 °C and 16.2% at 400 °C. | At 400 °C, melt-pool width increased by 35 µm and mean columnar-grain width by 16%; proof stress and UTS rose 26% and 25%, hardness rose 11.8%, and elongation fell 48.8%. Carbide size and occurrence increased with temperature and exposure time. | (maly2022effectofpreheating pages 12-13, maly2022effectofpreheating pages 1-2) |
| Inconel 718 | 50–500 | No general crack-free threshold follows from the cited studies; response is temperature- and process-dependent. | Experiments at 50–150 °C reported a 22% decrease in one stress component but a 13% increase in another. Modeling/other work indicated stress may decrease up to approximately 200 °C but increase again at 250–500 °C as microstructure and strength change. | Elevated preheat can enlarge/coarsen grains and alter yield strength; therefore the residual-stress response is not necessarily monotonic. | (maly2022effectofpreheating pages 12-13) |
| γ-TiAl, Ti–48Al–2Cr–2Nb | 800, inductive | At 800 °C, cracking was suppressed; ambient-temperature builds became unstable after roughly 10 layers, whereas the heated process deposited 50 layers without optically observed cracks. | Maintaining the bed and growing component hot, followed by controlled cooling at 5 °C/min, reduces thermal gradients and cold-cracking risk. | Apparent density exceeded 99%. The induction system sustained 800 °C for 450 min with approximately ±10 °C oscillation and could exceed 840 °C. | (caprio2020defectfreelaserpowder pages 11-14, caprio2018developmentofnovel pages 8-10, caprio2020defectfreelaserpowder pages 1-5) |
| CM247LC / MAR-M-247 | 550–570 | High-temperature preheating is reported as a principal crack-mitigation measure for this crack-prone γ′-strengthened Ni superalloy, though the available excerpt does not establish complete crack elimination. | Reduced thermal gradients are intended to lower distortion and residual stress; quantitative values were not available in the retrieved evidence. | Temperatures near 550–570 °C substantially change the thermal cycle and may promote in-situ microstructural evolution; the processing window remains alloy- and exposure-time-sensitive. | (maly2022effectofpreheating pages 15-16) |
| Tungsten | 400–600 | At 400 °C, tracks widened and higher thermal input improved interface behavior. At 600 °C, oxidation caused poor wetting, balling and highly variable tracks, offsetting the expected crack-reduction benefit. | Preheating and insulation reduced thermal cycling; laser pre-scanning raised mean plate temperature from about 75 to 225 °C and reduced central temperature fluctuation from more than 30 to about 10 °C. | A 600 °C bed was controlled within ±5 °C, but rapidly formed blue WO₃-type oxide repeatedly reappeared after laser ablation. Pre-scanning plus insulation increased mean fusion-zone penetration from about 72 to 88 µm. | (field2020laserpowderbedfusiona pages 206-214, field2020laserpowderbedfusion pages 206-214, field2020laserpowderbedfusion pages 199-206) |
| TiAl on EOS M 290 HT research system | Base plate up to 900; upper powder-bed surface up to 1200 | Combined plate and surface/chamber heating enabled dense, crack-free TiAl processing and avoided the loss of preheat effectiveness with increasing build height. | Heating the uppermost layer as well as the base reduces through-height thermal gradients more effectively than base heating alone. | IR-camera monitoring, chamber cooling and inert-gas purification were integrated; oxygen was maintained below 200 ppm. The high thermal exposure produced a fine lamellar γ-TiAl/α₂-Ti₃Al structure with a through-height microstructural gradient. | (wartbichler2022laserpowderbed pages 2-4) |


*Table: Quantitative comparison of LPBF preheat conditions and their effects on cracking, stress and microstructure. It distinguishes demonstrated outcomes from temperatures that were merely investigated or machine-limited.*

**Ti-6Al-4V.** Powder-bed preheating from 100 to 770 °C significantly reduced residual stresses (88.3% reduction at 470 °C, negligible residual stress at 570–770 °C), decomposed brittle α′ martensite to an α+β equilibrium, and improved mechanical properties—a 3.2% yield-strength increase and 66.2% ductility increase were reported (aydin2025theuseof pages 90-94, aydin2025theuseof pages 94-96).

Proof stress and UTS rose 26% and 25%, while elongation dropped 48.8%. Carbide-phase evolution was strongly linked to both temperature and build time (maly2022effectofpreheating pages 12-13, maly2022effectofpreheating pages 1-2).

**Inconel 718 (50–500 °C).** One study reported a 22% decrease in σ_z residual stress but a 13% increase in σ_x at higher temperatures; another found stress decreased up to ~200 °C but increased again at 250–500 °C as grain coarsening reduced yield strength (maly2022effectofpreheating pages 12-13).

At 600 °C, however, a blue WO₃-type oxide formed rapidly and re-formed after laser ablation, causing balling, poor wetting, and highly variable track widths—demonstrating the critical importance of atmosphere control at elevated temperatures (field2020laserpowderbedfusiona pages 206-214, field2020laserpowderbedfusion pages 206-214).

#### 1.3 Heater Technologies

The following table compares demonstrated LPBF preheating technologies:

| Technology | Maximum temperature achieved (°C) | System description | Advantages | Limitations | Source |
|---|---:|---|---|---|---|
| Resistive cartridge heaters | Typically ≤200 commercial; 700 custom | Six 100 W, 24 V cartridges heated a 5 mm tungsten plate over a 60 × 45 × 50 mm build volume. Two central K-type thermocouples provided ±5 °C switching control; a 30 min dwell promoted uniformity. A ceramic insert reduced downward heat loss. | Simple, compact, inexpensive and readily controlled; well suited to a swappable Ø25–50 mm aluminium-alloy plate module. | Conductive losses into the piston and frame can dominate; adjacent components require independent thermocouples and safety cut-offs. *Table: Comparison of demonstrated LPBF preheating methods, achievable temperatures, engineering architectures and limitations. The data distinguish practical aluminium-platform heaters from specialized high-temperature systems for TiAl, tungsten and ceramics.*

**Resistive cartridge heaters** are the standard technology. Commercial machines typically reach ≤200 °C, but a custom design for tungsten LPBF used six 100 W, 24 V cartridge heaters in a 60 × 45 × 50 mm build module, reaching a 700 °C target with ±5 °C control from two K-type thermocouples and a 30-min temperature-uniformity dwell (field2020laserpowderbedfusiona pages 272-279, field2020laserpowderbedfusiona pages 279-280). Aluminium-nitride ceramic heaters (3 kW, 290 × 290 mm) achieved only 374 °C on the plate when insulation was 44% efficient; redesigned thermal pathways were predicted to reach ~650 °C (ramulifho2022evaluationofa pages 3-5, ramulifho2022evaluationofa pages 1-3).

**Induction heating** reaches higher temperatures. The "Project Grisù" helical coil system sustained 800 °C for 450 min with ±10 °C oscillation and reached >840 °C, using a 48 V, 20 A supply at ~100 kHz. Three water-cooled exchangers protected vulnerable components, keeping them below 100 °C (caprio2020defectfreelaserpowder pages 11-14, caprio2018developmentofnovel pages 3-5, caprio2020defectfreelaserpowder pages 7-11). Earlier pancake-coil induction approaches achieved up to ~1000 °C (caprio2020defectfreelaserpowder pages 5-7, caprio2018developmentofnovel pages 1-3).

**Laser diode preheating** (4 × 1.25 kW diodes) operated at 625 °C and substantially reduced residual stress in 316L (ramulifho2022evaluationofa pages 3-5). CO₂ and Nd:YAG laser preheating reached 1500–2500 °C but only for ceramic processing (ramulifho2022evaluationofa pages 1-3, aydin2025theuseof pages 94-96).

#### 1.4 Thermal Isolation and Environmental Effects

Thermal isolation is critical: inadequate insulation and multiple metallic contact paths prevented one system from reaching its 600 °C target despite 3 kW heater power (ramulifho2022evaluationofa pages 3-5). The induction system used ceramic breaks and water-cooled exchangers, targeting motor/transmission temperatures below 70 °C and all piston components below 100 °C (caprio2018developmentofnovel pages 3-5). Argon was stabilized for at least 4 hours before heating to minimize oxidation risk (field2020laserpowderbedfusiona pages 272-279, field2020laserpowderbedfusion pages 279-280). At 600 °C, tungsten powder rapidly formed blue WO₃ oxide even with argon flooding, demonstrating that O₂ levels must be tightly controlled at elevated temperatures (field2020laserpowderbedfusiona pages 206-214, field2020laserpowderbedfusion pages 206-214).

---

### 2. Interchangeable Build Plates and Reduced Build Volumes

Several commercial and research machines implement small or interchangeable build volumes:

- **Sisma MYSINT100:** Features a Ø99 mm plate with twelve Ø12 mm removable inserts, each located by precision cylindrical pockets, alignment pins (Ø1.5 mm partial cylindrical holes), and reverse-side fixing screws. This design enables rapid restoration—the plate base can be reused by replacing utilized inserts with new or regenerated ones (zanini2024newmultifunctionbuilding pages 2-4).

- **Modular lab-scale LPBF (Schanz et al.):** A compact system (240 × 200 × 300 mm) with a Ø40 mm substrate plate, capable of handling up to four powder types. With a 0.5 mm build height, only ~791 mm³ of powder was needed for a complete parameter study of 16 five-millimeter cubes. Powder reservoirs were accessible and replaceable within 3 min, and recoating took approximately 5 s per layer (schanz2022individualprocessdevelopment pages 2-4).

- **Aconity3D MINI:** Used for research including biomedical porous structures, with small build volumes suited to exploratory builds (perino2024design3dprinting pages 48-56).

- **Zero-point clamping systems:** Provide rapid, reproducible fixation and maintain a common reference system between LPBF, robotic handling, and post-processing steps (khorasani2020areviewof pages 5-7, ferchow2022designandvalidation pages 3-5).

- **Circular platforms** limit powder dispersion and avoid powder filling/unloading during the build cycle, promoting a more homogeneous process (khorasani2020areviewof pages 4-5).

**Transferability of results:** Small build plates alter thermal mass, lateral heat loss, inter-layer time, and part spacing. AlSi10Mg preheating creates build-height-dependent ageing gradients that are sensitive to these thermal boundary conditions (chambrin2022insituageing pages 1-2). Therefore, results from small plates should be treated as screening evidence requiring production-machine correlation builds rather than direct qualification data.

---

### 3. Powder Supply Variants

**Gravity-fed and recirculating systems** are the two primary categories. In both, a metered volume of powder is delivered and spread by a wiper (rigid blade or roller) across the build area. The delivered quantity per layer is governed by the wiper-to-bed gap rather than by explicit mass dosing (revanur2024novelscanstrategies pages 18-22).

**Modular multi-hopper systems** have been developed for research. The Schanz et al. system accommodated four independently accessible rotating powder reservoirs; for a Ø40 mm plate and 50 µm layers, the geometric layer volume was approximately 628 mm³, with ~163 mm³ added for the density difference between powder bed and consolidated parts (schanz2022individualprocessdevelopment pages 2-4). An ORNL development feeder incorporated 16 small-scale hoppers for evaluating multiple refractory compositions (hyer2025strategiesforfabricating pages 1-7). Double-hopper systems with a lower mixing chamber enable blended compositions (schanz2022individualprocessdevelopment pages 1-2).

**Minimum powder per layer:** For a Ø50 mm plate at 50 µm layer thickness, the geometric layer volume is ~0.098 cm³. Accounting for powder packing (~50-60% apparent density) and a safety margin for overflow, the commanded dose is approximately 0.2–0.4 cm³ per layer (schanz2022individualprocessdevelopment pages 2-4).

**Powder changeover** on industrial machines can require up to two days for complete cleaning and replacement; multi-powder hoppers and automatic sifting/recycling systems significantly reduce this (khorasani2020areviewof pages 5-7).

---

### 4. Automation-Friendliness

#### 4.1 Build-Plate Exchange and Handling

Automated powder sieving and recirculation reduce operator involvement and production time. Build-plate exchange is accelerated through airlocks and rapid-transfer ports. Zero-point clamping systems enable rapid, reproducible fixation without manual tightening. Redundant build plates and rotating mechanisms enable reciprocal use, maximizing machine uptime. Switchable filter units and shared automatic powder-handling systems can serve multiple machines (khorasani2020areviewof pages 5-7, khorasani2020areviewof pages 4-5).

A sheet-metal clamping system demonstrated automated transfer between LPBF, robotic handling, and milling, using a universal disposable interface that avoided clamping forces on filigree structures (ferchow2022designandvalidation pages 3-5).

#### 4.2 Integration with Autonomous/Self-Driving Laboratories

The concept of AI-driven autonomous AM laboratories is rapidly developing. Zhao et al. proposed an AI Auto-Lab platform combining multi-hopper AM printing, robotic heat treatment, automated X-ray CT and mechanical characterization, and closed-loop optimization using Bayesian methods, reinforcement learning, and active sampling. An intelligent agent generates alloy compositions, recommends laser parameters via physics-informed models, and coordinates equipment through APIs (zhao2026alloydesignparadigms pages 12-13). Collins and Ales described an AM-enabled autonomous laboratory architecture using agent-controlled, semi-standardized cells with safety interlocks, MCP interfaces, and sample/information transport between cells. Human-in-the-loop supervision defines initial strategies and stopping conditions, while the system organizes experiments, ingests data, and terminates when objectives are met (collins2026additivemanufacturingenabled pages 1-2, collins2026additivemanufacturingenabled pages 18-20). These platforms can direct powder hoppers to AM systems, predict parameters from physics-informed neural networks, and use hardness indentation as an accelerated screening surrogate (collins2026additivemanufacturingenabled pages 18-20).

Self-driving laboratories for materials discovery emphasize modular automation, robotic sample handling, real-time monitoring (optical, thermal, acoustic, photodiode), and closed-loop control, with LPBF characterized as having high automation potential but challenging melt-pool physics (nowak2026highthroughputmethodsin pages 15-16).

---

AA7075 was not made crack-free even at 400 °C, so 500 °C capability is valuable but not universally sufficient. Literature-demonstrated values are distinguished from recommended engineering targets that still require system-level validation.*

#### Summary of Critical Design Targets

The most impactful design choices, in order, are:

1. **Heated build-plate cassette** capable of 500 °C (for crack-free 6xxx processing), with a routine 200 °C module for AlSi10Mg screening.
2. **Interchangeable Ø25/Ø50 mm build modules** with kinematic coupling repeatability ≤10 µm in Z.
3. **Thermal isolation** using ceramic breaks and water cooling to keep piston components below 70–100 °C.
4. **Reproducible plate registration** via three-point kinematic or zero-point coupling.
5. **Sealed powder-containment sleeves** matched to plate diameter with controlled thermal expansion clearance.
6. **Dual-zone temperature control** with ±5 °C stability and independent safety trip.
7. **Vacuum-purgeable argon chamber** maintaining O₂ <200 ppm (target <100 ppm for Al alloys).
8. **Quick-swap sealed hopper cartridges** (25–100 cm³) with RFID identification.
9. **Servo recoater** with ≤5 µm gap repeatability and force monitoring.
10. **Robot-compatible plate removal** with positive mechanical lock and presence sensors.

For crack-prone 7xxx alloys, 500 °C preheating alone is demonstrably insufficient (velikajne2026influenceofbase pages 8-11); grain refiners (e.g., Sc, Zr, TiB₂ additions) must be the primary crack-mitigation strategy, with preheating providing supplementary stress reduction. For AlSi10Mg, controlling preheat temperature precisely (150–170 °C vs. ambient) is essential because the in-situ ageing response is highly sensitive to both temperature and exposure time (chambrin2022insituageing pages 1-2, zhu2023microstructuralanalysisof pages 9-12). All screening results from small plates must be validated on production-scale builds because altered thermal mass, heat sinking, and inter-layer time change microstructural outcomes in ways that cannot be fully predicted from volumetric energy density alone.

## Design Review for a Desktop Alloy-Screening LPBF Machine

This review synthesizes the peer-reviewed literature on heated build plates, interchangeable build volumes, powder supply, and automation for laser powder bed fusion (LPBF), with specific attention to aluminium alloy screening. The findings are organized into four sections followed by a ranked list of concrete design choices.

---

### 1. Heated Build Plates in LPBF

#### 1.1 Preheat Temperatures and Effects on Aluminium Alloys

**AlSi10Mg (35–200 °C).** Platform preheating at 150 °C promotes in-situ precipitation during the build: granular Si and needle-like β″ precipitates form, increasing as-built strength but substantially reducing the subsequent T5 ageing response (pqac-00000007). At 170 °C, an in-situ ageing gradient develops with build height; a hardness peak occurs approximately 40 mm above the platform (corresponding to ~10 h of remaining build time), and material nearer the platform over-ages, exhibiting lower hardness and higher fracture energy (pqac-00000001). At 160 °C on an EOS M290, long exposure induced substantial over-ageing already in the as-built condition, reducing the best available hardness and tensile performance relative to cold-platform direct-aged material (pqac-00000046). The cold platform preserves higher Si supersaturation, making it more suitable for a subsequent direct-ageing strategy.

**EN AW 6182 / 6xxx (400–500 °C).** Preheating temperature had the strongest effect on hot cracking in LPBF of EN AW 6182. A columnar-to-equiaxed transition initiated near 400 °C, and at 500 °C with optimized scan parameters, crack-free parts with density >99.0% and a fully equiaxed grain structure were achieved (pqac-00000006).

**AA7075 / 7xxx (25–400 °C).** At 100 and 200 °C, preheating did not significantly reduce crack density or change grain morphology relative to room-temperature processing (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000002). At 400 °C, the crack network changed to columnar morphology with pronounced stress relaxation and reduced hardness, but cracking was not eliminated (pqac-00000003). Zn (~1 wt.%) and Mg (~0.3 wt.%) evaporated consistently regardless of preheat temperature (pqac-00000000). Separate work on AA7075 achieved 99.8% density at 200 °C without crack suppression (pqac-00000004). For AA6061, 500 °C preheating produced crack-free cubes, though divorced eutectic particles may limit post-ageing elongation below 5% (pqac-00000004).

**AA2024 / 2xxx.** The maximum reported preheating temperature was 200 °C, insufficient to suppress the strong hot-cracking susceptibility from Cu–Mg segregation (pqac-00000004).

The following table summarizes preheat effects across all alloy systems:

| Alloy system | Preheat temperature range (°C) | Key effects on cracking | Key effects on residual stress | Key effects on microstructure/properties | Source |
|---|---:|---|---|---|---|

#### 1.2 Preheat Effects on Non-Aluminium Alloys

**Ti-6Al-4V.** Powder-bed preheating from 100 to 770 °C significantly reduced residual stresses (88.3% reduction at 470 °C, negligible residual stress at 570–770 °C), decomposed brittle α′ martensite to an α+β equilibrium, and improved mechanical properties—a 3.2% yield-strength increase and 66.2% ductility increase were reported (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000036, pqac-00000037).

**Inconel 939 (RT–400 °C).** Unlike Ti and Al alloys, IN939 exhibited *increased* residual stress proxy (deformation) at high preheating: +4.2% at 200 °C and +16.2% at 400 °C. Proof stress and UTS rose 26% and 25%, while elongation dropped 48.8%. Carbide-phase evolution was strongly linked to both temperature and build time (pqac-00000033, pqac-00000035).

**Inconel 718 (50–500 °C).** One study reported a 22% decrease in σ_z residual stress but a 13% increase in σ_x at higher temperatures; another found stress decreased up to ~200 °C but increased again at 250–500 °C as grain coarsening reduced yield strength (pqac-00000033).

**γ-TiAl (800 °C, inductive).** Using an inductive preheating system at 800 °C, crack formation was fully suppressed and apparent density exceeded 99% for Ti–48Al–2Cr–2Nb. Without heating, the build failed after ~10 layers due to powder-bed instability and cracking (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000017, pqac-00000021).

**Tungsten (400–600 °C).** At 400 °C, weld tracks widened and interface quality improved. At 600 °C, however, a blue WO₃-type oxide formed rapidly and re-formed after laser ablation, causing balling, poor wetting, and highly variable track widths—demonstrating the critical importance of atmosphere control at elevated temperatures (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000040).

**TiAl on EOS M290-HT (900 °C base + 1200 °C surface).** A modified system combining 900 °C base-plate heating with up to 1200 °C surface heating of the uppermost powder layer produced crack-free TiAl with fine lamellar microstructure. The system maintained O₂ below 200 ppm using inert-gas purification, IR-camera monitoring, and chamber cooling (pqac-00000023).

**Resistive cartridge heaters** are the standard technology. Commercial machines typically reach ≤200 °C, but a custom design for tungsten LPBF used six 100 W, 24 V cartridge heaters in a 60 × 45 × 50 mm build module, reaching a 700 °C target with ±5 °C control from two K-type thermocouples and a 30-min temperature-uniformity dwell (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000011). Aluminium-nitride ceramic heaters (3 kW, 290 × 290 mm) achieved only 374 °C on the plate when insulation was 44% efficient; redesigned thermal pathways were predicted to reach ~650 °C (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000014).

**Induction heating** reaches higher temperatures. The "Project Grisù" helical coil system sustained 800 °C for 450 min with ±10 °C oscillation and reached >840 °C, using a 48 V, 20 A supply at ~100 kHz. Three water-cooled exchangers protected vulnerable components, keeping them below 100 °C (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000019, pqac-00000020). Earlier pancake-coil induction approaches achieved up to ~1000 °C (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000022).

**Laser diode preheating** (4 × 1.25 kW diodes) operated at 625 °C and substantially reduced residual stress in 316L (pqac-00000009). CO₂ and Nd:YAG laser preheating reached 1500–2500 °C but only for ceramic processing (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000015).

#### 1.4 Thermal Isolation and Environmental Effects

Thermal isolation is critical: inadequate insulation and multiple metallic contact paths prevented one system from reaching its 600 °C target despite 3 kW heater power (pqac-00000009). The induction system used ceramic breaks and water-cooled exchangers, targeting motor/transmission temperatures below 70 °C and all piston components below 100 °C (pqac-00000019). Argon was stabilized for at least 4 hours before heating to minimize oxidation risk (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000043). At 600 °C, tungsten powder rapidly formed blue WO₃ oxide even with argon flooding, demonstrating that O₂ levels must be tightly controlled at elevated temperatures (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000040).

### 2. Interchangeable Build Plates and Reduced Build Volumes

Several commercial and research machines implement small or interchangeable build volumes:

- **Sisma MYSINT100:** Features a Ø99 mm plate with twelve Ø12 mm removable inserts, each located by precision cylindrical pockets, alignment pins (Ø1.5 mm partial cylindrical holes), and reverse-side fixing screws. This design enables rapid restoration—the plate base can be reused by replacing utilized inserts with new or regenerated ones (pqac-00000045).

- **Modular lab-scale LPBF (Schanz et al.):** A compact system (240 × 200 × 300 mm) with a Ø40 mm substrate plate, capable of handling up to four powder types. With a 0.5 mm build height, only ~791 mm³ of powder was needed for a complete parameter study of 16 five-millimeter cubes. Powder reservoirs were accessible and replaceable within 3 min, and recoating took approximately 5 s per layer (pqac-00000050).

- **Aconity3D MINI:** Used for research including biomedical porous structures, with small build volumes suited to exploratory builds (pqac-00000047).

- **Zero-point clamping systems:** Provide rapid, reproducible fixation and maintain a common reference system between LPBF, robotic handling, and post-processing steps (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000048).

- **Circular platforms** limit powder dispersion and avoid powder filling/unloading during the build cycle, promoting a more homogeneous process (pqac-00000025).

**Transferability of results:** Small build plates alter thermal mass, lateral heat loss, inter-layer time, and part spacing. AlSi10Mg preheating creates build-height-dependent ageing gradients that are sensitive to these thermal boundary conditions (pqac-00000001). Therefore, results from small plates should be treated as screening evidence requiring production-machine correlation builds rather than direct qualification data.

---

### 3. Powder Supply Variants

**Gravity-fed and recirculating systems** are the two primary categories. In both, a metered volume of powder is delivered and spread by a wiper (rigid blade or roller) across the build area. The delivered quantity per layer is governed by the wiper-to-bed gap rather than by explicit mass dosing (pqac-00000027).

**Modular multi-hopper systems** have been developed for research. The Schanz et al. system accommodated four independently accessible rotating powder reservoirs; for a Ø40 mm plate and 50 µm layers, the geometric layer volume was approximately 628 mm³, with ~163 mm³ added for the density difference between powder bed and consolidated parts (pqac-00000050). An ORNL development feeder incorporated 16 small-scale hoppers for evaluating multiple refractory compositions (pqac-00000049). Double-hopper systems with a lower mixing chamber enable blended compositions (pqac-00000026).

**Minimum powder per layer:** For a Ø50 mm plate at 50 µm layer thickness, the geometric layer volume is ~0.098 cm³. Accounting for powder packing (~50-60% apparent density) and a safety margin for overflow, the commanded dose is approximately 0.2–0.4 cm³ per layer (pqac-00000050).

**Powder changeover** on industrial machines can require up to two days for complete cleaning and replacement; multi-powder hoppers and automatic sifting/recycling systems significantly reduce this (pqac-00000024).
